activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
story:
Jeremy would tell you, if you asked, that he was not hiding in the garage, and that he had chosen the garage simply because the light was best there, slanting through the dust-smeared window onto his grandmother's workbench, where he was building a pencil. This was true, as far as it went. The pencil was for his application portfolio, the one due in nine days, a drawing instrument he was carving from walnut and brass, and the light was good. He had the graphite cores laid out on a tea towel, thin black rods he'd bought at the art shop in town, and he was filing the brass ferrule to size when the door banged and his little cousin came in chewing the end of a yellow school pencil like an ear of corn.

"You're going to die," Jeremy said, mostly to see what would happen.

The cousin, who was eight and visiting because everyone was visiting, because the house had become the place where people went when there was nowhere better to be, took the pencil out of his mouth. "Fatima said there's lead in these."

"There is no lead in these." Jeremy set down the file. He had learned this last spring, in the hospital library of all places, flipping through an old chemistry book while machines upstairs did whatever machines did, and it had stuck in him the way odd facts do, like a stone in a shoe. He picked up one of the graphite rods and held it out. "Pencil lead has never been made of the metal lead. They only call it lead because back in the sixteenth century, when they found graphite, they thought it was a kind of lead ore. They were wrong. It's this. It's graphite. You can chew the whole pencil and you still won't get lead poisoning, though you'll get splinters."

The cousin took the rod, rolled it between his fingers, and put it in his mouth anyway, which struck Jeremy as the correct scientific response. Jeremy had been eight once too, though he would have said, then as now, that he was basically fine, that he had been inured to hospital waiting rooms from an early age and they no longer bothered him at all, which was why his hands were absolutely steady on the file, the small tremor being the incipient headache he'd had since Tuesday and nothing else.

River found them twenty minutes later, letting themselves in through the side door with the ease of someone who had been coming to this house since they were six. They sat on the workbench stool, watched Jeremy score a groove into the walnut halves, and did not say anything about the hospital, which Jeremy appreciated and also did not appreciate, because not saying anything about it was its own kind of saying. "That's going to be beautiful," River said finally, which was almost worse.

"Graphite," the cousin announced from the floor, where he was sorting Jeremy's spare cores by length. "Graphite, graphite."

"He's got it memorized now," Jeremy said. "You could give the tour."

River picked up one of the cores and held it to the light, and Jeremy watched them notice the way it shone, greasy and dark, the way metal was supposed to shine and never quite did. That was the thing Jeremy kept circling: people had looked at this stuff four hundred years ago and seen something familiar, slotted it into the world they already had, and the name had stuck long after the mistake was obvious. He thought about his own file, the essay he hadn't written, the form with the box that asked him to describe his home situation in fifty words or fewer. He was fairly sure he had not misidentified anything in his life. He was also fairly sure that was the kind of thing a person would be the last to know.

Fatima appeared in the doorway then, phone in hand, saying his grandmother wanted to know if he was coming inside, that his mom's antigen results had come back and they were, as far as anyone could tell, the good kind of number. She said it carefully, the way you'd set down a full glass. Jeremy nodded and kept filing, because the ferrule was a sixteenth of an inch too wide, and if he stopped now he would have to look at her face and she would have to look at his, and there were things about his face he was not prepared to have known.

He worked the brass down, fit the halves together around the graphite, and rolled the finished pencil once across his palm, dark and quiet as the thing it carried.

"Graphite," the cousin said again, and bit it.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The paper plate in Emma's hand had gone soft from the condensation of her cup, and she kept folding its soggy rim in smaller and smaller triangles while Ms. Liu carried out the last tray of burgers. The whole team was scattered across Brian's backyard, the net still strung between the poles his dad had sunk into the lawn four summers ago, though nobody was playing. It was the end-of-season party, which Emma had imagined would feel like a beginning, somehow, and instead felt like a paragraph that didn't know how to end.

Brian was by the cooler, holding court about the semifinal loss, the way he always did, reframing it as a kind of noble campaign. Emma had noticed this about him all season: he tended to valorize anything the team did, turning a Tuesday practice in the rain into a story about character, and usually she liked it, because it made ordinary afternoons feel like they counted for something. Today, though, the story had a hole in it, and the hole was the seniors.

Larry sat on the porch steps between two of them, both girls Emma had passed to for three years without ever learning their favorite music or their middle names. One of them kept saying "next year," and then stopping, and then saying "well," and then not finishing that either. Emma watched her twist a bottle cap into the grass until it disappeared.

"You're doing the face," Brian said, appearing beside her with two cups of lemonade, one of which he pressed into her free hand. "The face you do when you're about to say something in English class."

"I'm not. It's nothing." She drank the lemonade too fast. Then, because it wasn't nothing: "It's just weird. Ms. Liu had us read this thing in group dynamics, for the leadership unit. Bruce Tuckman. He had these stages a group goes through, forming, storming, norming, performing. Everybody knows those four. But in 1977 he and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth one."

Brian raised an eyebrow. "A fifth stage. What is it, injury?"

"Adjourning," Emma said. "It's for when a group's work ends and members separate." She hadn't meant to recite it like a flashcard, and her ears went hot, but Brian didn't laugh. He looked over at the seniors on the steps, and his whole performance-of-seriousness face dropped into actual seriousness.

"So we're in it," he said. "Right now. This is the stage."

"That's the thing, though. It's not a stage like the others. The other ones you pass through and come out the other side better. This one you just come out the other side." She gestured at the yard with her cup, the folded triangle of plate still pinched in her fist. "And I keep catching myself thinking we should be able to fix it, or honor it, or do it right, like there's a correct way to leave. And I don't think there is. I think you just do it and it's ugly a little."

Ms. Liu called them all over for the presentation of the game balls, one for each senior, and everyone gathered in the strange, sedimentary quiet of an ending, the season's layers pressing down on the moment: August two-a-days at the bottom, the road win in October, the loss last Thursday still soft on top. When the last senior got her ball, she held it the way you hold something you're about to give away, and nobody clapped right away, and then everybody clapped too long, trying to make the clapping fill the space where next season should have been.

Emma stood next to Larry afterward, both of them holding paper plates they weren't eating from. "You knew her the longest," Emma said. "Does it feel like anything? Like a real thing that's happening?"

Larry considered it, kicking at the corner of the porch step. "It feels like the day after a test," he said. "You know the grade already. There's just nothing left to study."

The seniors started a last game, just for fun, seven of them and anyone who wanted in, and Brian jogged toward the net calling Emma's name over his shoulder. She set her plate down on the railing, next to the bottle cap the senior had buried in the grass, and went.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The playground sat behind the elementary school, and the city had left one hoop up at the far edge of it, which meant Laura's rec team had claimed the cracked asphalt as its home court every Sunday since September. Today only half of them had come, and the empty swings creaked behind her in the wind while she waited for practice to count as started. Wade arrived fourteen minutes late, which was better than last week's absence and worse than the week before that, when he had simply not come at all and sent no message until Tuesday.

She had spent the bus ride over reading an article for her psych class, the kind her teacher assigned and half the class skimmed, and one paragraph had snagged her. The psychologist John Gottman distinguished a complaint from criticism: a complaint addressed a specific behavior, while criticism attacked the person's character. She'd read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to name something she had watched happen to this team all season without being able to say what it was.

Ariane had said it first, after the game on Thursday, in the parking lot with the car doors open and the lights on. "You always mess up," she'd said, meaning Wade, meaning the turnover in the last minute, meaning two years of standing around waiting for him. Laura had laughed along and then had not slept well, and she still wasn't sure why the laugh bothered her more than the sentence.

"All right," she said now, pulling the ball off her hip. "Three on three until the others show. Wade, you're with me."

They ran the drill she'd planned, the one Coach had scribbled on a napkin: outlet pass, sprint, catch at the elbow. Wade's passes came in hot and late, and Laura caught two of them with her chin and missed the third entirely. The plastic slide behind the fence had ionized the dry October air so badly that her hair kept lifting off her shoulders, clinging to the ball, and every time she wiped it back the anger came with it, wanting somewhere to go.

"What is wrong with you today?" she heard herself say, and Wade stopped, ball under his arm, and his face did the thing faces do when they decide to stop being open.

She called time. On the bench by the fence, an old man she knew only as Mr. Patel was sitting with his newspaper, the way he did every Sunday, close enough to hear everything and polite enough to pretend otherwise. Laura walked to the water bottle, took a long pull, and made herself think in sentences. Not what is wrong with you. What did you actually do? You missed practice twice. Your passes were late in this drill, this one, on this court, on this Sunday. The behavior, not the person. She turned the article's distinction over and found she could hold both ends of it at once: Ariane's frustration was real and worth listening to, and the shape Ariane had poured it into was a shape that Wade could do nothing with, because it told him what he was instead of what he'd done. Maybe both things were true. Maybe you could honor the anger and still refuse the weapon.

She walked back to half court. "Wade. You missed practice twice this month, and in that drill your passes came a full count late. That's the complaint. That's what I've got."

He bounced the ball once, twice. "That's cold," he said, but he wasn't leaving, and his shoulders had come down from around his ears. "The count thing's fair. The other thing, my mom's shifts changed. I should've texted."

"You should've texted," Laura agreed. "Ariane's going to have her say too, and she's not wrong to be angry, but I'm asking you to hear the drill part and not the 'always' part. The 'always' part isn't information. It's just weather."

He looked at her for a second, then at Ariane, who was standing under the hoop pretending to fix her shoelace and clearly listening. "Fine," Wade said. "Run it again. I'll hit you on time."

They ran it again, and this time the pass arrived early and soft, right into her hands at the elbow, and she laid it in off the glass. Mr. Patel turned a page of his newspaper. Ariane picked up the second ball and walked toward half court without a speech, without any peroration at all, which from Ariane was its own kind of apology. The team had gone nearly sectarian this season, two camps with Wade as the border between them, and Laura didn't know if one honest sentence could move a border. She only knew the next pass came on time, and the one after that, and after that one Ariane called out, without irony, "Again. From the top."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
story:
The sedan on the corner of the lot was seven years old and priced at eight thousand dollars, which was three thousand more than Justin had. He had counted the money twice in the parking lot, in an envelope, because the app on his phone showed a number he did quite trust. The salesman, a florid man named on his badge only as Al, had already said "monthly payment" four times before they reached the desk inside.

"Two hundred a month," Al said. "That's it. You're a student, you've got a job, the bank loves that."

Justin said he wanted to know the total. Al tapped his screen with the patience of someone who had answered this question before and found it unprofitable. Over five years, at the rate, the car would cost nine thousand four hundred. Justin wrote the figure on the dealership's notepad, under the eight thousand, and Al watched him do it the way a chess player watches an opponent move a piece he had forgotten about.

While Al went to check something with the manager, Justin called his brother, who was two years out of college and answering on the second ring because he was on a bus. Justin asked, half as a joke, whether a loan was a good idea.

"I owe more than I borrowed," his brother said. "I borrowed thirty-one thousand. I checked the balance yesterday and it's higher. Thirty-three and change."

"How?"

"Unpaid interest gets added to the principal," his brother said. "It's called capitalization. Then they charge interest on the interest too. I wasn't paying during school, so it piled up and got folded in, and now the pile earns its own pile."

Justin looked at the notepad. Two hundred a month felt small, but five years of five percent on money he hadn't paid yet would do the same thing his brother's loan had done, quietly, while he was thinking about something else. He asked what would happen if he paid the interest as it accrued instead. His brother said he hadn't thought of that until a year too late, and then the bus tunnel took the call.

When Al came back, Justin said he'd take the car for eight thousand cash, but he only had five. Al's expression went stoic. He said the bank couldn't do five down on this unit, and that payments could start at one-fifty if that helped. Justin said the one-fifty version cost even more in the end, because of capitalization, and Al paused, perhaps deciding whether to be pleased or worried that an eighteen-year-old had said that word in his office.

Maia was outside leaning on her bike when Justin emerged. She had told him last week that the whole dealership ran on people who looked at the monthly number and never the total, and she asked, with visible anticipation, whether he had signed something.

"I didn't sign anything. I'm going to wait, keep working, and buy it outright in the fall." He held up the envelope. "And my brother told me to put the five thousand in a savings account instead of the envelope. Same thing in reverse. The interest gets added, and then it earns interest on itself. It works for you instead of against you."

Maia said that was the first financially responsible thing she had ever heard him say, and that she was genuinely impressed, and that she had to go because she was late. He watched her wheel her bike across the lot, past the row of sedans, and stop at the bright orange convertible by the service entrance, the one with the big red bow, the one whose sticker he had glanced at earlier and decided not to think about. She had a job interview here next week, she'd mentioned, in the office. He stood by the doors of the dealership as she rang the bell, and through the glass he heard Al's voice, warm and unhurried: "Two hundred a month. That's it. You're a student, you've got a job, the bank loves that."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
The bleachers at Whitfield's field rose in silver tiers, and from the top row you could see the whole stadium plus a strip of parking lot where the marching band kids smoked behind their parents' cars. Lily had chosen that top row on purpose, in a text she had typed and deleted twice before sending: "Want to sit high up? I like seeing the plays develop." Kiran had replied in nine minutes, which felt like a reasonable interval, neither desperate nor indifferent: "Sure. I'll bring hot chocolate."

"You're staging this," Teresa said, unwrapping a burrito she had smuggled past the ticket table. Teresa had insisted on coming, on the grounds that a first date at a school event needed a witness. "Candles at dinner would be hedonistic enough, but you're adding altitude. You're designing an experience."

"I'm not an egoist," Lily said, which was not what Teresa had said, and both of them knew it. "I just want to know if it's real."

"Real like what?"

Lily didn't answer, because the honest answer involved a paragraph she had read in October, sprawled on her bedroom floor with a psychology textbook she'd borrowed from Ms. Sadeghi's classroom shelf out of boredom. In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge. She had read it three times, the way you read something that seems to be about you personally. The page had not explained it, and she had liked that, the bare strangeness of it, a fact sitting there like a stone. She remembered thinking: so a heart pounding from fear and a heart pounding from liking someone are not distinguishable from the inside. She had been seventeen then and it had seemed like trivia. Now she was eighteen and had a date in eleven minutes and it seemed like a warning.

Kiran texted at 6:52: "At the gate. The cashier wouldn't take my ticket because I printed it at home and it's basically a gray rectangle." Lily laughed out loud, then felt Teresa watching her laugh, then felt self-conscious about being observed feeling something, which was the whole problem in miniature.

They climbed. Kiran carried two hot chocolates and apologized twice for the gray rectangle. The top row swayed a little in the wind, more than Lily had expected, a low thrum under the metal like a struck tuning fork, and when the home team fumbled and the crowd surged to its feet, the whole structure shifted and Kiran grabbed the rail with a small, honest sound of alarm. Lily's own pulse went up, sharp and immediate, and there it was: the pounding, the heat in her palms, the exact signature of what she had felt last Wednesday when Kiran had leaned over her lab notebook and their shoulders had touched. Indistinguishable. She watched Kiran's profile against the floodlights and tried to sort the feeling into its two possible sources and could not, and understood suddenly that she might never be able to, that this was maybe the deal with all of it, every crush and every friendship and every decision she was about to make about colleges and cities and distance.

"So I have to tell you something," she said, and her mouth had gone so dry it felt as though the October wind had climbed the bleachers specifically to desiccate it. "There's this study. 1974, these researchers Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron. Men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge."

"Call her," Kiran repeated slowly. "Like, ask her out."

"Like ask her out. I read it in a book Ms. Sadeghi keeps on her shelf. And I picked the top row because of it. Which I realize now might make me a manipulative egoist, engineering a scary bridge and then checking whether I like you or whether I'm just scared." Teresa, four rows down and pretending not to listen, snorted into her burrito.

Kiran was quiet through the next play, a touchdown that neither of them watched properly. Lily braced for the polite withdrawal, the diplomacy of someone deciding she was too much. "Okay," Kiran said finally. "Then neither of us knows anything, because I've been terrified since Tuesday when you asked me, and I can't tell if I like you or if I just like being done being terrified." Lily laughed again, and this time she let Teresa hear it, and below them the band struck up and the top row hummed like a held breath. Kiran held out the second hot chocolate, still steaming, and Lily took it.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
Zachary turned eighteen at midnight, which meant that by breakfast he was, technically, a citizen of full standing, though the pancakes tasted the same. His mother had left a sticky note on the microwave that said go do it, underlined twice, and beneath it a second note, in his stepfather's handwriting, that said bring ID. This struck Zachary as ominous in a way he could not articulate, so he folded both notes into his wallet and walked to the community hall with Coraline, who had turned eighteen in March and had been insufferable about it ever since.

The hall smelled of floor wax and coffee that had been sequestered too long in its urn, developing a character all its own. A folding table blocked the entrance, and behind it sat a woman with a clipboard and the posture of someone who had already argued with eleven people that morning. Emiliano was already in line, holding a paper cup and radiating the patience of a man who had arrived at six forty-five on principle.

"You're late," Coraline said, though they were fifteen minutes early.

"I'm ceremonial," Zachary said. "First election. I wanted to arrive at a dignified pace."

The line moved in lurches. Ahead of them, Mr. Grewal from three doors down stood with his jacket buttoned wrong, one hole off, which Zachary noticed and elected not to mention. Mr. Grewal taught shop at the middle school and had once rebuilt Zachary's bicycle wheel for free, refusing payment with the phrase it's what neighbors do, a currency Zachary had never known how to convert. He had a doctor's appointment at ten, he told the man in front of him, loudly enough that the whole line was invited to consider it, and the whole line politely declined the invitation.

When Zachary reached the table, the woman ran her finger down the printed list, then back up, then down again, as though his name might have migrated in the interval. "It's not here," she said. "Are you registered?"

"I registered at the DMV. In August. The man said it was automatic."

The woman's face performed a small, tired pantomime of sympathy. "The man says a lot of things. You can still vote. Since the Help America Vote Act, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot. It goes in this envelope, and it counts only once officials confirm you're eligible."

Emiliano leaned over Zachary's shoulder. "So it's arbitrage," he said. "You cast the vote now and settle the paperwork later. You're betting your registration is real."

"It's not a bet," Coraline said. "It's his right."

"It's both," Zachary said, and surprised himself by meaning it.

He filled out the affidavit at a side table, the pen chained to a clipboard, which gave his signature a hostage quality. The paper asked for his address, his date of birth, the last four digits of his Social Security number, and, in a final flourish, an oath that he was who he said he was. He thought about the two notes in his wallet, one from each parent, and understood for the first time that they were not really about identification.

The provisional ballot itself looked ordinary, which was somehow the insult. Everyone else slid their ballots into the scanner and heard the satisfying thunk of participation, and his went into a manila envelope that the woman sealed, signed across the flap, and set in a gray bin with maybe nine others. A locked cover came down over the bin. His vote had been cast and simultaneously shelved, both real and pending, like a package marked out for delivery and held at the depot.

Mr. Grewal was still behind him, checking his watch. "They'll count it," he said, low enough that only Zachary heard. "I did one of those two years ago, moved precincts, and they counted it. You follow up, that's all. You call the county office, you give them the number on your receipt." He tapped the stub in Zachary's hand as if tapping a shoulder. "I'd do it myself, but I've got a doctor's appointment at ten, and if I miss it I have to wait another month, and at my age a month is not a small thing."

"That's exactly what the appointment is for," Mr. Grewal said. "The tectonic stuff. It's all shifting under there, whether anybody's watching or not. You just make sure they watch yours." He stepped up to the table, produced his license, and was, within ninety seconds, entirely on the list.

Outside, Coraline had her I VOTED sticker placed at a deliberate angle, like a medal or a brand depending on the light. "Does it count?" she asked.

"If they confirm I'm eligible," Zachary said. "Which I am. So yes. Probably. In a few days."

"That's a lot of hedging for a democracy."

He held up the receipt and read the number aloud, twice, until Coraline repeated it back, and then he texted it to himself as well, because he was eighteen now and had learned, in his first hour of civic life, that the system trusted you only as far as your paperwork went, and that trust beyond paperwork was a private matter. The coffee urn, visible through the propped door, gurgled.

Emiliano drained his cup and pointed at Zachary's receipt. "So call them Thursday."

"Thursday," Zachary said, and put the number in his front pocket, where he could feel it.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Victor had been sitting in the waiting room of the clinic for twenty minutes when Rayne dropped into the chair beside him, hood up, backpack still on, as though planning to leave before anyone could ask him a question. They had Ms. Lombardi's peer health seminar together, the elective that everyone signed up for because it filled the graduation requirement without a final exam, and Ms. Lombardi had decided that the curriculum would not stay abstract. She wanted each student to instantiate the material, her word, in an actual conversation with an actual person, and Victor's appointment for his college physical had seemed like the obvious chance.

"I'm not here," Rayne said. "Tell anyone you saw me and I'll deny it."

"Nobody's asking you to confess anything. I have to practice explaining stuff anyway." Victor held up the folded sheet of paper with his three assigned topics printed at the top: consent, contraception, where and how to get tested. "You want to be my audience?"

Rayne looked at the paper the way people look at a form they intend to leave blank. "I feel fine," he said. "That's my whole answer. I feel fine, so I don't need any of it."

Victor recognized the argument, because it had been his own until two weeks earlier. His father used the same logic about dental appointments, and Victor had never had a cavity, which seemed to prove something. But Ms. Lombardi had sent them to the county health department's website, which sat open in Victor's laptop like an archipelago of small islands, each one a separate fact he hadn't known existed, and some of the islands had unsettled him.

At the desk, the receptionist slid a clipboard across to Rayne without comment. Rayne wrote his name, then stalled at the section asking about conditions present since birth. "Congenital," he read. "What does that even mean here?"

"Like if you were born with a heart thing," Victor said. "Or sickle cell. It's asking what you came in with, not what you caught."

Rayne checked no and shoved the clipboard back. When the nurse called his name, he stood up too fast, then stopped in the doorway. "You can come," he said, not quite looking at Victor. "Since you're rehearsing or whatever."

The exam room was small and smelled of soap and paper. The nurse practitioner, whose badge read only a first name, asked her questions in a flat, quick rhythm, and Rayne answered most of them in monosyllables until she said they'd do a urine test, since he'd asked for one, sort of, by showing up.

"I only asked because he made it sound like a thing you do," Rayne said, tilting his head at Victor.

The nurse didn't lecture. She said only, "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms at all, so a test is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." Then she handed him the cup and left, and the sentence just sat there in the room with them.

"So feeling fine," Victor said slowly, working it out as he said it, "doesn't prove anything. It's not evidence. It's just a feeling." He had half-thought he was reciting something; instead the logic landed on him for the first time, personally, the way a fact about someone else becomes a fact about you.

"Yeah," Rayne said. "Thanks. That's very comforting." But he took the cup and went down the hall.

While Rayne was gone, the nurse came back for Victor's own physical, and afterward she printed a card with the clinic's walk-in hours and slid it across the desk. "For your project," she said. "Or for you. Those aren't different categories, whatever your teacher told you."

In the parking lot afterward, Rayne stuffed the card Victor had copied for him into his back pocket without looking at it, and they stood a moment in the cold between the two cars. Rayne's results would be ready in three days, and he hadn't said whether he'd check them, and Victor hadn't asked. He would text him on Thursday, he decided, and Rayne would answer or not, and Victor would be left holding all these newly acquired islands of knowledge with no certainty about who wanted to live on them.

"Same time next year," Rayne said, unlocking his car, "remind me not to feel fine."

Victor watched the taillights pull out onto the road, the little card of walk-in hours still warm in his hand.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
story:
Aaron had written his ten-minute play in one sitting, which he took as proof of his genius, and then spent four days not rereading it, which he took as proof of his wisdom. The play was about the night his father missed his championship swim final because the car wouldn't start, which was true, except that Aaron had upgraded the car to a broken-down motorcycle and the missed final to a missed Olympic trial, on the grounds that truth was better when it was taller. Ms. Mendoza had said the assignment was "a moment from your own life," and Aaron had decided that a moment and a monument were close enough.

The problem was the table read. Hannah had cornered him outside the drama room with the class sign-up sheet, and when he asked what a table read actually was, she looked at him the way you look at someone who has been living in a cupboard. "It's a seated read-through of the script by the cast," she said. "You hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins. No moving around. Just voices." Aaron nodded as though he had known this all along, and then went home and lay on his bedroom floor for an hour, imagining his lines in other people's mouths, an experience rather like imagining your diary being read aloud at assembly.

"Recruit your actors," Ms. Mendoza told the class on Thursday, "and be kind to them, because they are donating their reputations." Aaden had already been drafted, on the strength of a voice that could make a cafeteria announcement sound like a declaration of war. Hannah took the role of the mother, and a quiet girl from second period took the narrator, because Aaron had written a narrator, which Hannah called "a bold choice for someone who doesn't trust the audience to keep up." Aaron said the narrator was epicurean, savouring every line, and Hannah said that was not what that word meant, and Aaron said it was now.

They gathered on Friday after last bell, around the scuffed table in the back of the drama room where the theatre kids ate lunch and left their sweaters to colonize. Aaron sat at the head with his pages, feeling ceremonial. Aaden slid into the chair beside him, cracked his knuckles like a safecracker, and said, "If my character is a misanthrope, I'm playing him as a man who loves everyone but pretends not to, because that's more tragic." Aaron said his character was not a misanthrope, he was just tired, and Aaden said, "Same thing, different bedtime."

The read-through began, and within ninety seconds Aaron's genius began to die. The motorcycle monologue, so noble in his head, sounded like a man explaining a warranty. The line "I would have swum the ocean for you, son" made Hannah laugh so hard she had to put her pages down, and even the quiet narrator girl winced, politely, the way you wince at a relative's joke. Aaden's big speech, the one about engines and fathers and the cruelty of machines, was genuinely good, and it transfixed the whole table, but the good parts made the rest sound worse, like a real flower in a bouquet of plastic ones.

"Nobody talks like this," Hannah said, not unkindly, tapping the page. "When your dad missed your final, what did he actually say?" Aaron began to say something heroic and stopped. What his father had actually said was, "I'm sorry, kiddo, I'll get the bus next time," and then he'd stood in the doorway in his work shirt, holding the keys, and Aaron had said it was fine, and gone upstairs, and it had not been fine, and nobody had said anything else about it ever. That was the whole moment. It was small and it was worse than the motorcycle.

He rewrote it that weekend, cutting the narrator entirely, which Hannah received as a personal victory. The new version was seven minutes, not ten, and mostly silence and short sentences, and at the second table read nobody laughed, and Aaden said the quiet parts were loud, and Hannah said nothing, which from Hannah was a standing ovation. On Monday Aaron told Ms. Mendoza he'd found the truth by listening to it out loud, and she said, "That's the assignment," in a tone that suggested the assignment had been outsmarting students for years.

Staging came next, and here Aaron overreached one final time: he decided the father should sit in a real chair at the edge of the stage, engine keys in hand, while the son swam nowhere, in air. It was, he announced, metaphorical. Ms. Mendoza let him build it. On performance night the chair transfixed the audience, a lone kitchen chair under one light, and Aaron watched from the wings with his heart going like a clock. Afterward his father found him in the hallway, keys still in his jacket pocket, and said, "Good play. Who's the guy on the motorcycle?"

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
story:
The letter had come on a Thursday, and by Friday morning Eve had sequestered herself in the guidance office's orange plastic chair, holding the envelope the way you hold a moth, gently, in case it decided to be alive again. Mr. Korhonen's office smelled of toner and old coffee. Through the frosted window, the hallway made its usual noises, lockers and laughter, the ordinary machinery of a school that had already stopped being about her.

"Congratulations," Mr. Korhonen said, reading the letter twice. "That's a strong program. Early Action, right?"

"That's what it says."

She had applied in October mostly to get her mother to stop saying the word "panic" in November. The admissions office had taken until mid-December to answer, and the answer was yes, and she had expected to feel finished. Instead she felt like a student who had proven one lemma and was now being told the theorem still had four pages to go.

"So that's it, then," said Tony, who had wedged himself into the doorway on his way to somewhere he would claim to have been going. "You're done. You got in. Why are you in here looking like you failed a driving test?"

"Because I'm not done. That's the thing. I looked it up last night, at like two in the morning." She laid a printout on the desk, a page from the college's own admissions site, one paragraph highlighted in anxious yellow. "Early Action isn't Early Decision. It gives you an early answer, but it's non-binding. If they admit you, you can still say no."

"Then say no. Or say yes. That's, like, two options, and you have until May."

"May," Mr. Korhonen confirmed, "for everywhere else too. The regular deadlines are all still open."

Tony made a sound that meant he considered this a good thing. Eve considered it the opposite of a good thing. She had budgeted her whole autumn for one plan, and the plan had been built on the assumption that December would end something. Now December had ended nothing, and the applications she had half-drafted in a notebook, the school in the city with the physics program she liked better, the one Tony was applying to, the one near her grandmother, all of them were suddenly real again, and due January first. Two weeks. The whole thing was due in two weeks, and the application fees sat in her checking account like a hostage situation.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," she said, and she stood up, because sitting in the orange chair made thinking feel like sinking. "My mom's side is, you have an acceptance, a real one, take it, stop spending money on lottery tickets. And she's not wrong. That's a whole perspective. It's prudent."

"And the other side?"

"The other side is that I got lucky once and I'm treating the luck like it's a character trait. The physics program is genuinely better at Halloway. I visited. I sat in the back of a lecture and understood maybe a third of it and wanted to understand the rest, which is more than I can say for anywhere else I've visited. But Halloway's regular decision rate is brutal, and if I don't finish those essays by January first, the question answers itself."

Mr. Korhonen laced his fingers and, to his credit, did not give a speech. "So finish the essays," he said. "The acceptance doesn't expire while you're writing them. Nobody from the other school is going to show up at your house."

"That's exactly what a person from the other school would say if they existed," said Tony, and Eve laughed for the first time in what felt like days, one of those evanescent laughs that shows up in a crisis, does its small work, and vanishes before you can be grateful for it.

She picked up the letter and slid it back into its envelope, then set the envelope face down on the printout, the yes covering the highlighted paragraph, both of them still true at once. "Okay," she said. "I'm finishing the Halloway essays. All of them, by the first. If I get in, I'll actually decide, like a decision, with the two options next to each other. If I don't, I go where I got in, and I don't get to wonder if I quit because quitting was easier."

"And if you get in and can't decide?" Tony asked.

"Then I'll be exactly where I am now, but in April, and slightly taller." She shouldered her bag. "I need my notebook. It's at Lachlan's, and he's had it since Tuesday because his printer works."

"You're going to Lachlan's to write four college essays in two weeks," Tony said.

"I'm going to Lachlan's to write three," Eve said. "The fourth one's about a moth, and I already have the first sentence."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In Judaism, a day begins at sundown, so a Seder or a Sabbath dinner is held on the evening that starts the holiday, not the evening that ends it.
story:
The message came in the family group chat at four in the afternoon, from his aunt: If Alexander is leading tonight, we'll be there at six. He read it twice, standing in his grandmother's kitchen with the sink running and the parsley still gritty in the colander, because he had told everyone the Seder was tomorrow night. He had planned the whole thing around tomorrow. The brisket his uncle was bringing was still at the butcher's, the charoset was not made, and the Haggadot, the ones his grandmother had used for forty years, were still in a box he had not opened.

He called Quinn first, because Quinn was the only person he knew who would stay calm about a calendar. "Okay," Quinn said, "when you told them the date, what did you say?" "I said the fifteenth. Everyone said the fifteenth. I put it in the calendar app." There was a pause on the line, the kind that presaged either a solution or a disaster. "And the first night is listed as the fifteenth?" "Yes." "So why does your aunt think it's tonight?" "Because tonight is the fourteenth," Alexander said, and then he said it again, slower, and the parsley sat in the colander and the water ran and ran.

He had known this once. His grandmother had said it every year, offhandedly, while lighting candles: the day starts at sundown, so the holiday starts on the evening before the date on the calendar. He had nodded at twelve, at thirteen, at fourteen, the way you nod at weather. Now it mattered, and he stood in her kitchen feeling the full weight of a fact he had owned and never used. Tonight, the evening that began the fifteenth, was the Seder. Tomorrow night would be the second night. He had booked the community hall for tomorrow, for the family that would not fit in the house, and paid the deposit with money from his tutoring job.

Kelsey arrived at five with the box of matzah she'd been asked to bring, took one look at his face, and put her keys back in her pocket instead of leaving. "Tell me," she said. He told her, all of it, while he chopped apples and walnuts for the charoset with a knife that felt too large. "So call the hall," she said. "It's Friday evening, someone's there for the bingo setup." He called. The custodian who answered was kind but immovable: the hall was reserved tonight by the seniors' club and tomorrow by his own booking, and no, he could not swap them, and the deposit was nonrefundable. Alexander thanked him and hung up and pressed his palms flat on the counter.

"We do it here," Kelsey said. "All fourteen people." "There are eighteen." "Then eighteen. Your grandmother's table extends." It did extend; he had forgotten that, the leaves stored behind the coats in the hall closet, a judicious piece of engineering his grandfather had installed decades ago. He pulled them out while Kelsey texted the group chat on his behalf, because his hands were shaking too much to type. Correction, she wrote, in her flat, no-nonsense way. Seder is tonight at six, at Grandma Ruth's. Bring whatever you have.

Then Ms. Cohen from next door knocked, holding a covered dish, because word traveled fast on that street. "I saw the lights and the cars," she said. "Is it tonight? I thought you'd booked the hall for tomorrow." "I did," Alexander said. "I got the evening wrong." She looked at him for a moment, and he waited to be corrected, or worse, pitied. Instead she said, "So the fifteenth starts at sundown, and you start tonight," set the dish on the counter, and began peeling the apples he had abandoned. "My mother did this in a kitchen half this size. What else needs doing?"

What else needed doing was everything. His uncle arrived at five forty with the brisket only half smoked, having pulled it off the smoker in a panic, and declared it would finish in the oven, an improvisement he defended with the fervor of a man who considered himself the family's resident epicure and took the pale brisket as a personal wound. Cousins carried chairs up from the basement. Alexander's father found the Seder plate in the cabinet and handed it over without a word, which was somehow both a relief and a heavier thing than instruction would have been.

At six, when the sky outside the windows had gone the color of the wine he was about to pour, eighteen people found seats, and Alexander opened his grandmother's Haggadot and saw her handwriting in the margins, small corrections and arrows, forty years of her leading this exact meal. He took a breath and began, and his voice cracked once on the first blessing, and no one looked away or made it strange. He asked the Four Questions the way she used to, inviting the youngest cousins up beside him, and his aunt passed the parsley, and Ms. Cohen, who had lived next door for thirty years and never once come inside, was seated at the corner as though she had always been there.

The brisket, out of the oven at last, turned out fine. Somewhere around the second cup of wine, his uncle began taking credit for it. Alexander let him. There would be, he understood now, another Seder tomorrow night, at the hall, the one he had booked in error, and he did not yet know whether to cancel it or to let it stand, a second gathering he had arranged by accident and might arrange on purpose. He looked down the length of the extended table, at the candles burning low in their holders, and his grandmother's Haggadot open in front of him, her handwriting pointing the way to the next page. "Wash your hands," he said, and reached for the cup.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
story:
Gabriella spread her notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with saucers because the window was open and the lake wind came through in long, patient gusts. The essay was due Monday, and Mr. Whitaker had written one line at the bottom of her draft: "You can describe the policy but you cannot yet explain it." Her laptop sat among the saucers, its battery icon orange, and her grandmother moved behind her with a dish towel, drying the same pot she had already dried.

The question was simple to state and impossible for her to answer. Why does raising interest rates slow inflation. She understood the pieces separately: rates go up, borrowing costs money, people buy less, prices stop climbing so fast. But when she tried to write the chain down, each link felt like an assertion rather than a reason, and Mr. Whitaker, who read essays the way a jeweler reads a hallmark, had noticed.

She had come to the lake house for the quiet, and for her grandmother's cooking, and because Sidney had texted that the library was full of seniors weeping over their own applications. Sidney had also sent a voice memo that Gabriella played now, tinny through the laptop speakers: "Okay, my dad says think of it like a fever. Rates are the medicine. That's it, that's the whole metaphor, good luck." Her grandmother, folding the towel, said, "That's a terrible metaphor. Medicine cauterizes a wound. Interest isn't a burn."

Gabriella laughed, then stopped, because her grandmother had gone back to the stove and the remark sat there, half accidental. She turned it over. A burn that stops a burn. High rates were a deliberate small harm, applied to cauterize a larger one, and the honesty of that framing was what her draft lacked. Her version pretended the policy was painless. But she still couldn't say how anyone would know when to stop, how a central bank could tell whether its burn was finished.

She typed a question into the search bar, and the reading was dry and prolix, committee statements and testimonies that went on for pages saying almost nothing. Then, on the Federal Reserve's own website, she found it, plainly stated, almost buried: on January 25, 2012, the Federal Reserve had adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, feeling the small exhilaration of a lock turning.

"Grandma," she said. "Listen to this. Personal consumption expenditures price index. That's how they measure it. And two percent, that's the target. But here's the part I don't get. Two percent isn't zero. Prices still go up. Why is that winning?"

Her grandmother set down the towel and came to the table, reading over her shoulder with her glasses on the end of her nose. "You're asking why success still costs something," she said. "Ask your grandfather. He asked that about my cooking for forty years." She tapped the screen once, above the date. "But that number didn't always exist, dear. Somebody chose it, on a day, in a room. That's your answer, or the start of one."

Gabriella sat with that. The target was a decision, not a law of nature, and a decision could be argued with, could be two percent instead of zero for reasons she could investigate and still find unpersuasive. She opened a new document and began again, and this time the chain held together because it ended somewhere: rates rose to slow inflation toward the announced goal, and the goal itself was a policy choice made on a specific day by specific people, which meant the whole apparatus was human, contestable, responsible. She wrote for an hour while the wind moved the saucers and her grandmother made soup, and when Ian called to ask whether she'd finished, she read him her middle paragraph aloud.

"Okay," Ian said, "but would two percent actually be fine for you? Your tuition goes up every year anyway."

"I don't know," Gabriella said. "That's the part I can't settle. Maybe a little inflation is healthy and maybe it's just slow bleeding that nobody counts because everyone agreed on the number first." She looked at her draft, at the margin where she had written the date in her own handwriting, January 25, 2012, as if pinning a specimen. She could defend the mechanism now, most days, and she could say where her certainty ran out, and Mr. Whitaker had asked for exactly one of those things, though she suspected the second was the harder one to give.

Her grandmother set a bowl of soup beside the laptop and stood a moment, reading the screen upside down. "You've written 'uncertain' four times," she said.

"I know," Gabriella said. She picked up the spoon.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Transport costs shrink the gains from comparative advantage, and if shipping a good costs more than the difference in production costs, trading it no longer pays.
story:
The flyer went up on Monday outside Mr. Flores's room: regional economics competition, teams of three, topic this year was trade. William copied the details into his notebook before the bell, because the scholarship attached to it was the kind of thing his mother taped to the refrigerator without comment, which was how he knew she was counting on something.

He signed up with Yann and Taylor, neither of whom had taken economics. Yann wanted the scholarship for the same reason William did. Taylor wanted to win arguments. Their first practice, held at the folding table outside Yann's garage where they were also selling lemonade for a summer fund, collapsed in eleven minutes.

"So Portugal makes wine cheap and England makes cloth cheap," Taylor said, tapping the textbook. "Portugal should make wine, England cloth, and they trade. Both get richer. Done. What is there to argue?"

"That's absolute advantage," William said. "Comparative advantage is different. It's about what you give up." He reached for the words and found them thin. "Even if one country is better at making both things, it still pays for each to make the thing it's comparatively better at, and trade for the rest."

Yann frowned. "That can't be right. If you're better at everything, why buy from me?"

It was the exact question the judges would ask, and William could feel the answer slipping. He looked down at the lemonade stand, at the half-empty pitcher and the lemons Yann's cousin had driven across town to buy that morning because the shop there sold them cheaper. Taylor was counting the cash box.

"How much did the lemons cost?" William asked.

"Six dollars. The place near school charges nine for the same bag."

"And the gas?"

Taylor pulled the receipt out of the box. "Five fifty."

The three of them sat with that. Six dollars plus five fifty was eleven fifty, which was more than nine, and the lemonade fund had just lost two fifty to a bargain. Yann laughed once, without much humor in it.

"There it is," William said. "Comparative advantage is real, the lemons really are cheaper across town, but transport costs shrink the gains, and if shipping a good costs more than the difference in production costs, trading it no longer pays. The theory's true and we still lost money. Both things at once." He wrote the sentence down on a napkin, then again in his notebook, because it felt like the spine of something.

The next practice, they tried to parametrize the whole argument: production costs on one axis, shipping costs on the other, a line where trade stopped paying. Taylor built the numbers fast and dirty, demanding William justify each one, and William caught himself defending assumptions he'd made an hour earlier without thinking. He stopped, crossed two out, and started over. The work had a grim exhilaration to it, the feeling of a structure holding weight it hadn't been tested against.

At the mock round, Mr. Flores judged. He listened to their case, then pushed. "So free trade is a scam when shipping's expensive?"

"No," William said. "It's narrower than that. Trade pays when the cost gap between two producers is bigger than the cost of moving the goods between them. Sometimes it is, sometimes it isn't. You have to check, both sides, every time." He paused, honest about the edge of it. "We still don't know how you'd predict the shipping costs before they move. That part we can't do yet."

Mr. Flores wrote something on his pad and didn't show them.

At the competition itself, the opposing team ran the textbook line, Portugal and England, both countries gain, full stop. In cross-examination Taylor asked their speaker one question: "What's it cost to get the wine to England?" The speaker blinked, started a sentence about efficiency, and stopped. The judges leaned forward. William's team placed second, which came with a smaller scholarship and a plaque Mr. Flores hung outside his door the following week with a strip of tape.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Yann elbowed him. "Second."

"Second," William agreed. He turned the plaque over in his hands, feeling the cheap weight of it, and decided it was worth exactly what they'd earned. On the drive home his mother asked how it went, and he said, "We found out what we don't know," and she nodded like that was an answer.

That Saturday they ran the lemonade stand again. Taylor walked to the corner store and came back with a bag of lemons, receipt in hand, and spread it flat on the table for all of them to see.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: In the balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water.
story:
The kitchen clock said 9:40 and Charlie had a chemistry exam at eight the next morning, which meant the mole problems had to surrender before she went to sleep. She spread her notes across the counter between the toaster and her mother's herb garden, three pots of basil going leggy by the window, and found the worksheet Ms. Clarke-Williams had handed back with a red circle around question four. "Given 4.0 grams of hydrogen gas, how many moles of water form?" The circle was not angry, only insistent, the way Ms. Clarke-Williams was insistent in the lab, walking between the benches with her arms folded, waiting for students to notice their own mistakes.

Charlie had been coasting on pattern for most of the semester, copying the shape of solved examples the way a beginning pianist copies fingering, and it had worked until it didn't. The test was different because the reactant was hydrogen and the product was water, and the bridge between grams and moles had to be built from the balanced equation itself, which she had until now treated as decoration, something written above the problem like a title. Her phone buzzed on the counter. Vienna again.

"Did you get four," the message said. "I got four and it felt too easy."

Charlie typed back that she hadn't gotten anything yet, then set the phone face down beside the sugar bowl. Her mother came in for water, glanced at the papers, and asked whether Charlie wanted tea, and Charlie said no, thank you, and her mother left without pressing, which was one of her mother's quiet virtuoso performances, the knowing when not to hover. The kettle went on anyway. In the silence after the door swung shut, Charlie pulled the notebook closer and wrote the equation at the top of a fresh page, slowly, the way Ms. Clarke-Williams made them write it in lab: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.

She counted atoms on both sides because counting was the only thing she trusted herself to do without a formula. Left side: four hydrogen atoms, two oxygen atoms. Right side: four hydrogen atoms, two oxygen atoms. The equation balanced, which meant it was telling her something true about proportions, and she sat with that for a moment, chewing the end of her pen. Two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water. She said it out loud to the empty kitchen, testing it, and the basil did not object.

So the equation was a ratio, not a decoration. If she had grams of hydrogen, she could convert to moles using the molar mass, and the equation would tell her how many moles of water came out the other end, like a machine whose gears were numbers. She looked up hydrogen's molar mass in the table at the back of her book, wrote it down, and did the division with the calculator, and then the multiplication the ratio demanded, and arrived at a number that was not four. It was twice four. She checked the arithmetic twice, and it held.

She picked up the phone. "I got eight," she wrote. "Two moles of hydrogen make two moles of water, not one. You used the ratio upside down or something." There was a long pause while Vienna, across town in her own kitchen, presumably metabolized this. Then: "wait." Then: "WAIT." Then a photograph of Vienna's notebook, the wrong line crossed out in green ink, the correct one beneath it, and beneath that a small triumphant drawing of a water molecule wearing a crown.

Charlie copied the clean solution into her notes, and found she could feel where the logic bent, the exact hinge where grams became moles and moles became product, the way you can feel the weld in a piece of ductile metal if you run a thumb over it. There were still things she couldn't do, whole regions of the review sheet she hadn't touched, acid-base problems and something called limiting reactants that she suspected would not limit itself to one evening. She was honest with herself about that at least, and it felt less like failure than like a map with the roads drawn in and the rivers still blank.

She stacked the papers, drained the tea her mother had left anyway, and rinsed the cup. At the doorway she stopped, went back, and tore the page with the corrected solution free of the notebook, folding it once and putting it in the pocket of her hoodie, where she could take it out on the bus in the morning. The kitchen light went off with its small click.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
Christian's grandmother had planned her own funeral down to the receipt, and the receipt was the problem. Taped inside her recipe box, on a card in her slanting hand, she had left instructions: a burial, not cremation, a specific plot in Rosehill Cemetery beside her sister, and marigolds on the grave by the first of November. "Not later," the card said. "It matters more than you think." His mother had read it twice, handed it back, and said she had to go argue with the insurance people, who claimed the policy had lapsed and were offering a settlement that would, in their phrasing, indemnify the family against any further claims, which meant they wanted this to be over. Christian was left with the flowers. He had until sunset, because the flower seller at the weekend market packed up at five, and tomorrow was the first, and the card had been clear.

He took Adam, because Adam had a car and because Adam never asked questions until they were already parked. In the lot behind the hardware store, under strings of paper flags, an old woman was selling buckets of orange marigolds, so many that the air smelled like a struck match dipped in honey. Christian reached for the bucket of yellow roses beside them, cheaper by half.

"Don't," Adam said. "The card said marigolds."

"The card said marigolds because she liked marigolds. She's dead. She won't audit the arrangement."

"You don't know that's why it said marigolds."

Christian put the roses back. It was a specious argument, he knew, the kind he made when he wanted permission to do the easy thing, and Adam's flat look said he knew it too. Christian counted his money. The marigolds were twelve dollars a bundle, and he needed three bundles, and he had thirty-one dollars, which his mother had left for gas and lunch.

Alexis was already at the market, which saved him a phone call. She worked Saturdays at her aunt's stall two rows over, bags of dried chiles and rolls of paper stamped with skeletons, and she knew the flower woman, whose name was Ofelia. Alexis walked over with her aunt trailing behind, took one look at the card in Christian's hand, and stopped smiling.

"She wanted them for the first," Alexis said. "Not for the funeral."

"The funeral's the first."

"The funeral's the fourth. Look at your phone." He looked. The burial was scheduled for the fourth, because that was the earliest the cemetery could open the plot beside her sister, ground conditions, paperwork. The first was tomorrow. "So you put the flowers there tomorrow," Alexis said. "Before."

"Before the casket's even in the ground."

"That's not how it's supposed to go." Her aunt said something in Spanish, and Alexis answered, and then turned back to Christian with the expression of someone translating more than words. "Tomorrow is Day of the Dead. The marigolds, the orange ones, they're called cempasúchil. You put them on the graves because the color and the smell are supposed to lead the souls home."

Christian stood there holding the card. His grandmother had never once explained herself, not about the lapsed insurance, not about the thirty years she'd sent money to Guadalajara every December, not about why she kept her sister's photograph face down after 1994. He had assumed, in the lazy way he assumed things about her, that her instructions were preferences. Taste. Now it seemed possible they were navigation.

"Her soul," he said. "You believe that literally?"

"I believe you have thirty-one dollars and need three bundles and Ofelia closes at five."

The negotiation took four minutes. Alexis argued in Spanish, fast and low, and Ofelia crossed her arms and then uncrossed them and finally gave Christian three bundles for twenty dollars because, Alexis reported, his grandmother had bought sugar skulls from her stall for years and had once corrected her Spanish grammar in front of customers and Ofelia had hated her a little and respected her a lot. Christian paid. The clock read 4:41.

Alexis drove her aunt's van to Rosehill because Adam's car was leaking something and the cemetery was forty minutes across town and the light was already going amber at the edges. They arrived at 5:20, which was fine, because a cemetery keeps no hours that matter, but the ground was hard and the wind was up and the flowers kept wanting to lie flat. Alexis stood at the foot of the empty plot while Christian laid the stems along the stone marking her sister's grave and then, after a pause, along the raw earth where the casket would go on the fourth.

From the path, an older woman in a raincoat watched them work. She had come, like half the visitors that evening, with her own armful of orange, and she had stopped because the boy was doing it wrong, laying the flowers in neat rows like a groundskeeper, like mulch. She waited until he stepped back, then walked down and scattered what he had arranged, loose, reckless, a broken line of orange drifting from the road toward the headstone.

"It's a path, not a blanket," she said. "They follow it." She nodded at the stones down the hillside, where other families had done the same, orange threads unspooling in the last light. The boy looked at the trail she'd made, then at his own hands, then at the girl beside him, who was already pulling stems from the third bundle.

Christian worked until the bundle was empty. He could not make himself believe what the woman believed, and he could not make himself disbelieve his grandmother, who had never written an unnecessary word in her life. So he laid the flowers, and the wind moved them, and the line held, more or less, all the way to the road. Alexis crouched and fixed one stem that had rolled. "There," she said. "She'll find it."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
Brayden's poster read "Equilibrium: The System That Pushes Back," and he had spent the last hour watching people walk past it toward the volcano two tables down, which burped orange foam every eleven minutes to reliable applause. His own demonstration was quieter: two sealed flasks of pale pink solution on a hotplate, waiting for a temperature change nobody seemed interested in providing. Kingston had promised to come by at ten, and Kingston was across the room explaining to a middle schooler that the volcano's lava was "basically dish soap," with the authority of a connoisseur who had built three identical volcanoes himself and placed second every time.

Andrea arrived first, carrying a coffee she defended against the no-food rule by keeping it below table height. "So what does it do," she said. "Does it explode."

"It changes color."

"What color."

"Pink to blue, if I heat it. Blue to pink if I cool it." He turned the hotplate on. "The reaction can run forward or backward, and temperature decides which way it leans. That's the whole thing."

Andrea sipped her coffee. "So it's a mood ring."

"A mood ring would be an upgrade," Brayden said, and she laughed, which he counted as a win, because Andrea had spent all of junior year treating his chemistry enthusiasm as a mild affliction, like an allergy to pollen.

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya stopped at his table at quarter past ten, clipboard against her hip. She was judging the physical sciences section, and Brayden knew her reputation: she had once told a robotics team that their machine was "adequate, which is the most dangerous word I know." She looked at the flasks, then at the poster, then at him. "Who is Le Chatelier," she said, reading the small print at the bottom of his title.

Brayden opened his mouth and discovered that he did not know. He had copied the name off a website two nights ago, along with the diagram, because the diagram was clean and the name looked official. Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya waited with the patience of someone who already knew the answer, which was the worst part. His phone was in his pocket. He took it out, typed the name, and read what came up while the pink solution behind him began, slowly, to go blue.

"The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier," he said, "who stated it in 1884." He looked up. "I should have known that before I put his name in twelve-point font."

"Probably," said Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya, and made a note on her clipboard that he could not read upside down.

Kingston materialized at half past, drawn over not by loyalty but by the fact that the volcano had been unplugged for a safety inspection, and its presenter was remonstrating with a volunteer about whether foam counted as a fire hazard. Kingston watched Brayden move the blue flask onto a tray of ice. "So the cold one goes back to pink," he said. "What if you did both at once?"

"You'd get one of each."

"What if you did it halfway?"

"Then you'd get something halfway," Brayden said, and then, because Kingston's face had gone speculative, "It's not a bit, Kingston. It's a gradient."

Andrea leaned in as the cold flask began its return, blue draining out of it the way dusk drains out of a sky, in no single place you could point to. "It's actually kind of nice," she admitted, and then, quickly, "Don't tell anyone I said that about chemistry."

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya came back on her second pass while both flasks sat in transition, neither pink nor blue, each holding its position against the temperature being applied to it. "So," she said. "Which way does heating shift it?"

Brayden looked at the hot flask, blue and settled, and at the cold one going pink, and at the phone still open in his hand, and understood that he could say the color and nothing more, or he could admit the shape of what he actually knew. "Toward the blue side, in this system," he said. "Whether that's forward or backward, I'd have to check my equations again, because I mostly learned this by watching the flasks, and I don't want to tell you something I can't back up."

She wrote something longer this time. Across the room, the volcano was plugged back in, and the middle schooler's foam began to rise. Kingston drifted toward it like a man returning to the scene of a previous crime.

"Mr. Reyes," Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya said, using his last name for the first time. "The ice tray is leaking on my floor."

Brayden looked down. A thin ribbon of water had crossed the tiles and was pooling, unhurried and indifferent, around the toe of her shoe. He picked up the tray with both hands and went looking for paper towels.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
Brayden had promised his Spanish teacher he would try, which was easy to promise in April and harder to honor in July, in a rented flat above a bakery in Granada, where the fans turned the hot air without cooling it. The neighborhood association held its debates on Thursday nights in the back room of a cultural center, and Mr. Janssen, the retired Dutch professor who owned the flat and had befriended Brayden's mother over the listing, had suggested Brayden attend as a listener. Brayden went as a listener exactly once. On the second Thursday he put his name on the slate, because his five minutes were scheduled for the following week and he wanted to feel what the room felt like from the chairs.

The question for debate was whether the city should cap tourist apartments in the old quarters. Brayden had opinions, most of them inherited from his father, who liked lower prices and fewer rules, and some from Morgane, a French student he'd met at the bakery who lived above three vacation rentals and could not sleep in August. He spent three evenings drafting in a notebook, crossing out sentences, asking the cashier at the market whether his grammar was wrong and she would laugh and fix one word and hand him his change. He learned to say "housing" without stumbling. He learned that five minutes was much longer than he had imagined.

On the night, the room held perhaps forty people, a small podium, a bell. Morgane came with two flatmates and sat near the back, waving once. When Brayden's turn arrived he stood, gripped the edges of the podium, and began, and for the first ninety seconds his Spanish was slow and deliberate, each clause placed like a stone in a wall. He argued that the cap protected neighbors, that a neighborhood was not only a market, and that a city which sold every window to visitors would eventually have no one left to visit.

Then the man speaking against him, a property manager named on the program as the third speaker, took the floor and smiled with genuine warmth. He said, in Spanish, that it was charming to hear such conviction in the accent of a boy who had flown here on a budget airline and would fly home in two weeks. He said that perhaps the young man from the United States could tell them all what his own neighborhood in America had done about housing, if it had done anything at all. The room laughed, not cruelly, the way a room laughs when it is relieved. Ninety seconds remained on the clock, and the property manager spent them on the accent, the airline, the youth, and offered nothing about the cap.

Brayden sat down with his ears burning. Morgane caught his eye across the room and mouthed something he couldn't read. In the break, while paper cups of coffee circulated, he stood near the water pitcher and turned the moment over. The man had not answered him. That was the thing. He remembered his debate unit from junior year, the posters on the wall, and the word came back to him whole. He found Mr. Janssen by the door, who had watched it all, and said, quietly, testing it, "That was an ad hominem. He attacked me instead of my argument."

Mr. Janssen sipped his coffee and said only that the rebuttal period came after the break, and that Brayden had two minutes. He did not say what to do with them, which Brayden understood, later, as the whole gift.

When the bell rang for rebuttals, Brayden stood and kept his voice level. "An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself," he said, in Spanish, slowly enough that every syllable landed, "and in formal debate it is treated as a fallacy. So I will answer the parts that were arguments, and I will let my accent stand." He restated the cap, conceded that enforcement would be difficult, conceded that tourism fed families in this city including probably the man's own, and said that both things could be true at once and a policy had to choose which harm to bear. He said he did not know which harm was greater; he was eighteen and a guest. He sat down with eleven seconds left.

Afterward the property manager shook his hand and told him his subjunctive was better than his opponent's, which Brayden suspected was generous. Morgane waited by the door with her flatmates and asked whether he had really planned the fallacy line or found it in the moment, and he admitted, honestly, that he had found it somewhere between the water pitcher and the bell, and that he was not sure he would find it again under pressure. Outside, the street was still warm and full of people from many countries carrying gelato. She pointed up at a dark window three floors above a souvenir shop and said that was the flatmate who could not sleep, that he had taken to wearing earplugs to dinner.

"Then he should come next Thursday," Brayden said. "Tell him I'll save him a seat."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Table salt, sodium chloride, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole.
story:
The kitchen scale read 233.76 grams, and Mia stared at it as if it might confess to something. Her science fair project was due in nine days, and the whole design rested on a number she did not yet have: how many moles of sodium chloride were sitting in the plastic bag on her counter. She had promised Ms. Chea a proposal by Friday, complete with calculations, and so far she had a bag of salt, a borrowed scale from the chemistry room, and a growing suspicion that she had agreed to something beyond her.

"Are you still doing the salt thing?" Kathleen had asked her at lunch, not unkindly. "Lexi's doing a survey project. Hers took one afternoon."
