Lexi's project was about hand washing in the school bathrooms, a small piece of amateur epidemiology, counting who lathered and who rinsed and calling it data. Mia had almost switched to something like that herself, something answerable with a clipboard. But Ms. Chea had looked at her draft and said, "You keep avoiding the quantitative part. That's usually a sign it's the part worth doing." The sentence had landed with tectonic slowness, shifting something under the surface of Mia's plans that she hadn't fully mapped yet.

She opened her chemistry notebook to the page where she'd copied the reference values in class. Table salt, sodium chloride, has a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole. She'd underlined it twice back in September, the way she underlined everything then, before she understood which facts did the heavy lifting. Now, at the counter, she weighed the bag again and wrote the number on the back of an envelope: 233.76 grams. She divided. The pencil moved through the arithmetic slowly, and then she sat very still, because the answer was four. Exactly, cleanly, four moles.

"It's four," she said out loud to the empty kitchen. She checked it twice, dividing 233.76 by 58.44 both directions, running the multiplication backward to confirm. Four moles in the bag. She felt the particular satisfaction of a door that had been locked all semester suddenly swinging on oiled hinges. The number was not approximate, not a guess dressed up in significant figures; the universe, or at least the arithmetic, had cooperated.

Her mother came in for a glass of water and found Mia arranging the salt in a line of small piles on a sheet of wax paper. "How much did that cost you?" she asked, nodding at the salt.

"Eighty-nine cents," Mia said. "For four moles. Which means one mole costs about twenty-two cents." Her mother raised an eyebrow, and Mia laughed. "It sounds ridiculous, I know. But that's the point. Everything becomes countable. I couldn't count salt before, and now I can."

Her mother dried her hands and left her to it, and Mia sat with the envelope in front of her, weighing something less tangible. Kathleen's voice surfaced in her memory, the argument from lunch: that numbers like these were arbitrary conversions, a currency you had to exchange into and out of, a way of making the world fit the grid. And underneath that, her own older instinct, the one that had wanted to do the survey project: that the important things were patterns and stories, the shape of behavior, not its mass. She had spent years treating those two ways of thinking as rivals, the way people treat precision and imagination as opposites. Sitting at the counter with her four neat piles, she began to suspect they were more like two doors into the same room. The counting did not replace the wondering; it gave the wondering something to stand on.

Not that everything was settled. She still did not know whether the experiment itself would show anything, whether four moles of salt in her solution would behave differently enough from three to measure with a kitchen thermometer. She wrote "uncertainty" at the bottom of the envelope and, after a moment, left it there instead of crossing it out. Some of it she would amortize across the nine remaining days, a little doubt paid down each evening; the rest she would simply carry.

She texted Kathleen a photo of the four piles with the caption "countable now," and Kathleen replied with a string of exclamation points and "explain tomorrow." Mia put the kettle on, set the envelope where she would see it in the morning, and began repacking the salt into the bag, one careful pile at a time, weighing each before she poured it back.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
Alexia had signed up because the form said community food bank, and she imagined a basement with shelves, her handing cans across a counter. What the form neglected to mention was the farm. At seven on a Saturday morning she stood at the end of a picked-over squash field with Juliana and Aya, mud on her sneakers, while a coordinator handed out gloves and a clipboard with a requisition slip for crates, three per volunteer, no more. Juliana took her clip and asked, quietly, whether this counted as the full forty hours or whether they were being scammed.

"It's called gleaning," Aya said, reading the laminated sheet taped to the truck's tailgate. "We harvest what's left in the field after the main harvest. Food that would otherwise go to waste." She said it flatly, the way she read everything, and then bent and picked up a butternut squash the size of a newborn, half-hidden under a slashed vine. Behind them the coordinator called that the regular crew had already been through, and that what remained was theirs.

Alexia had expected waste to look like rot. Instead the field was full of sound vegetables, misshapen or slightly small or simply missed by the machine, and the more she found the stranger it felt. She filled her first crate in twenty minutes. Her second took longer, and by the third she was crawling on her knees through the rows, pulling fruit out of the cold furrows like Easter eggs, her breath fogging in the montane air that had come down overnight and settled in the low places of the field. Juliana worked the next row over and said nothing for a long time, which itself was information. Juliana had been the one who wanted the food bank, who had talked about it at lunch with real feeling, direct service, people not produce, and now here they were with produce and no people at all.

The crates went into the truck bed, and the truck went down the valley to a seniors' residence where the food bank ran a monthly table in the common room. Ms. Ma, who organized the table, met them at the loading door with a wheeled cart and a face that suggested she had done this many times and would do it many more. "Squash keeps," she said, turning one over in her hands. "That matters more than you'd think." She wanted, Alexia realized over the next hour, not just the food but the performance of it, the residents seeing young people carry things in, the table looking abundant. Twice she rearranged the squash into a pyramid, and twice a resident's walker bumped it askew.

The residents came through in a slow line. An old man took one squash, weighed it in both hands, put it back, took a smaller one. A woman with a cardigan over her shoulders asked Alexia whether she was Ms. Ma's daughter, and when Alexia said she was a volunteer, the woman nodded as though that were the more interesting answer and asked where the squash had come from. Alexia started to say the store, then stopped. "A farm," she said. "We picked it ourselves. It was left over after the harvest, so it would have gone to waste." The woman looked at the pyramid, then at Alexia, and said, "My father did that. Whole families, after the machines came through." She did not explain further, and Alexia did not ask her to.

Between residents, Juliana found her by the coffee urn. "This is not what I signed up for," Juliana said, but without heat, almost wondering. "Although look at that guy." The old man had come back through the line and was choosing a second squash, and Ms. Ma was letting him, pretending to be busy with the napkins. Juliana watched him for a moment. "Okay," she said. "Maybe it's what I signed up for and I just had the picture wrong."

Alexia had been turning something over in her mind the way Ms. Ma turned the squash, testing for soft spots. She had come wanting to give her time directly, face to face, and she had spent the morning on her knees in cold dirt instead; and yet the dirt was the reason there was anything to give, the unglamorous half of the work that made the visible half possible. Both were true at once, and she could not rank them, and she suspected she never would, and that this might be fine. The only bathos was her sneakers, which were ruined, and which she had thought, putting them on that morning, were her volunteering shoes.

Aya appeared with an empty cart and the clipboard. "There's a second field," she said. "The coordinator says cabbage, if we want it before noon." Juliana looked at her watch. Ms. Ma, across the room, was rebuilding the pyramid. "Cabbage," the old man said, not to anyone in particular, holding his second squash against his chest like a football. Alexia pulled her gloves back out of her pocket.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The turf at Miller Park still held the morning's rain, and Brooke's cleats darkened at the toes before warmups even began. She had made the county league team in March, the last cut surviving only because another girl tore something in her ankle, and every practice since had felt provisional, a borrowed coat she kept expecting someone to reclaim. Today the cones were set for passing triangles, small and close, nothing like the full-field sprints she had trained for all winter.

Hillary arrived late, hair still damp from a shower she had clearly rushed, and stood at the edge of the grid while the coach counted off groups. She had taken a knock to the temple eleven days ago in the game against Fairview, sat out two weeks, and been cleared by her doctor on Tuesday. Brooke knew this because Hillary had announced it in the group chat with a row of exclamation points, and because Mr. Sutton, who coached from a folding chair with a thermos and a laminated sheet he consulted like scripture, had said only, "We'll see how you go."

They started with jogging laps, then simple footwork, then short passes inside the triangles. Mr. Sutton called the drills out in an order that seemed almost ceremonially slow, and Brooke, waiting her turn, noticed the laminated sheet taped along the back of his chair. She drifted near it under the pretense of retrieving a ball. It was a return-to-play protocol, six steps printed in bold, beginning with rest and ending with full contact, and a line beneath in smaller type: the athlete moves to the next step only while free of symptoms. Beside the sheet hung a pencil on a string and a chart with Hillary's name at the top, checkboxes marching down the margin.

"You're the coach's acolyte now?" Gwenyth said, jogging past her with the ball. "Reading his clipboard like it's the oracle."

"I'm learning things," Brooke said. "Step three is light drills. Hillary's on step three."

The triangles were going well enough that Mr. Sutton widened them, calling for longer passes, more movement, and it was there, midway through a give-and-go, that Hillary pulled up. She didn't fall or grab her head. She simply stopped, one hand hovering near her temple like a person trying to recall a forgotten word, and walked to the sideline. Brooke followed, ostensibly for water.

"It's back," Hillary said. She said it flatly, the way you report weather. "Not bad. Like a band around it."

Brooke looked at the sheet in her memory, then at the actual sheet, twenty feet away. "You were on light drills," she said slowly. "The passing stuff. But he widened it. Longer passes, running onto the ball. That's more than light."

"So?"

"So the whole thing only works if you stay symptom-free to move up. If the headache comes back, you go back a stage. Not to the beginning." She was assembling this as she spoke, the printed steps arranging themselves in her mind like rungs on a ladder, some climbed, some now unclimbed. "You don't just push through to the next day because the doctor signed a form."

Hillary looked at the cones, at Gwenyth already reorganizing the drill, at her own shoes. "Two more weeks and the season's half over," she said. "I already lost the Fairview game."

"I know." Brooke did know; she had taken Hillary's starting spot in that game and had not enjoyed it, exactly, had enjoyed it and then felt the enjoyment curdle. "But the sheet doesn't care about the Fairview game. It just says symptoms, then back a step."

Mr. Sutton rose from his chair, thermos in hand, and came over before either of them could decide anything further. He looked at Hillary's face for a long moment, then at the chart on his chair, and Brooke watched him draw a single line through the third checkbox with the pencil on its string. "Tomorrow we start you at the easy passing," he said, which was all he said. He didn't lecture. He simply reseated himself and resumed calling the drill, though he narrowed the triangles back to their earlier size for everyone, quietly, without announcing why.

The rest of practice ran on toward dusk. Sticks of light came through the pines at the park's edge and lay across the wet grass like something scattered. Brooke took her turns, hit one pass badly and one beautifully, and found herself thinking about the ladder again, not as rules imposed but as a kind of honesty, a way of letting the body report the truth without argument. She had spent the season wanting so fiercely to belong on this team that she'd have played through anything, and she understood now that this wanting and the protocol were two different vocabularries for the same player. Which one you followed on a given Tuesday was a choice, but only one of them could be made twice.

Walking to the parking lot, Gwenyth caught up to them, unclipping her shin guards as she went. "That was perspicacious of you, by the way," she said to Brooke. "Figuring out the whole chart from one glance. Mr. Sutton's been doing this fifteen years and nobody's ever read it."

"I want to say something smart back," Brooke said, "but I mostly just didn't want Hillary gone again."

Hillary shouldered her bag. "Easy passing tomorrow," she said. "You're doing the triangles with me."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street, an early example of spatial analysis.
story:
Alexandra set the laptop on the kitchen table between the fruit bowl and her mother's nursing shift schedule, and opened the mapping software for the third evening in a row. The tutorial called it a geographic information system, and by now she could load the layers: the city boundary, the parcels of housing, the river's old floodplain rendered in patient blue. What she could not yet do was the thing Ms. Baptiste had actually asked for, an overlay showing which neighbourhoods sat inside the flood risk zone, and her first attempt had produced a map where half the city appeared to be underwater, including the hill her school stood on. Clearly something was wrong with the data, or with her, and she could not tell which.

Her mother came through in her uniform, scraping her hair back, still talking about the clinic. "They ran out of the rapid antigen tests again," she said, hunting through the drawer for a pen, "so we're back to sending people across town. Same people who have no car, of course." She kissed the top of Alexandra's head and left for nights, and Alexandra sat looking at the closed door, because that was the exact shape of the problem Ms. Baptiste kept circling in class: who gets sent across town, and why.

She called Adelyn, who answered with her phone propped against a stack of bio flashcards. "Tell me you fixed the flood layer."

"I fixed it," Alexandra said. "The water layer was in the wrong coordinate system, so everything was shifted north by like a kilometre. But now I have the real map, and it's worse. The flood zone is basically the east side. The east side is the housing they built cheapest, and it's a hundred-year floodplain, and nobody put that on a brochure."

"Put what on a brochure?" Adelyn said, but she was only half listening, muttering membranous organelles to herself.

Alexandra muted her and turned back to the screen. The overlay worked now. Where the blue flood layer crossed the tan housing parcels, the software darkened them into a bruised purple, whole blocks of it, and the map she had thought would be a technical exercise had quietly become something else. It transfigured numbers she already knew, a percentage here, a median income there, into a single visible shape you could point at.

Her introduction was due tomorrow and she still needed an opening, something older than her city, some proof that a map could change a mind instead of just decorating one. She typed "history of mapping disease" more or less as a joke, and the result arrived so fast she felt she must have known it somewhere already. She read it twice, then called Ava, who actually picked up. "You know what I found?" Alexandra said. "In 1854, this physician, John Snow, mapped cholera deaths in London, and they all clustered around one water pump on Broad Street." She scrolled the article with one hand. "It's basically the first spatial analysis. He didn't argue with anybody. He just showed where the deaths were, and the pump was in the middle."

"Wait, so they shut off the pump?"

"They took the handle off, yeah." Alexandra was already reordering her slides in her head, Snow's map first, then her own bruised purple blocks. "That's what I want mine to do. Not tell people what to think. Just put the two things on top of each other and let the shape show."

She worked until eleven, and when her grandmother wandered out, querulous about being unable to sleep, Alexandra made her tea and let her stand behind the chair. "That's our church," her grandmother said, tapping the screen, her finger landing square in the purple. "And your Aunt Rosa's old street is right there, just below it." Alexandra zoomed in and found the parcel, and the little outlined rectangle sat entirely inside the floodplain, the way it had sat there, unmarked and unremarked, for forty years.

In the morning she would present, and she could already imagine Ms. Baptiste asking what her map proved, whether flood risk caused the housing pattern or merely coincided with it, and Alexandra had decided she would say she didn't know yet, that the map showed where but not why. But it showed where with a clarity no one at City Hall had bothered to publish, and she had printed two copies, one for the classroom and one, folded into thirds, for the community meeting her grandmother mentioned on her way back to bed.

She saved the file twice, closed the laptop, and set it on top of the printed map by the door.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
Daniel spread the flashcards across the picnic table in his backyard, weighting the corners with pinecones because the wind kept lifting them like small stubborn animals. Glycolysis. Pyruvate. The Krebs cycle. Tomorrow was the unit test, and his grade in Ms. Haddad's class sat at a C plus, close enough to a B that he could taste it, far enough that he couldn't.

"Okay, so glucose gets split in the cytoplasm," Giovanni said, tapping the first card with a pen. "That's glycolysis. Two pyruvate. Then what?"

"Then the pyruvate goes into the mitochondria and the cycle happens." Daniel said it fast, the way you say something to get it over with.

Jayden, sprawled on the grass with his own deck of cards held above his face, squinted at them. "Why is it called the Krebs cycle? Did a guy named Krebs just, like, own it?"

Daniel started to say he didn't care, that names didn't matter, that the test was on the pathway not the history. Then he stopped, because a thought had snagged in him. He pulled out his phone and typed the name.

"Hans Krebs," he read. "He described the citric acid cycle in 1937, with a guy named William Johnson. And Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize for it."

"Shared it," Giovanni repeated, as if the word were a small insult. "With who?"

Daniel scrolled. It didn't say, or he couldn't find it fast, and something about that unsettled him, the way a missing piece of a jigsaw does, the sky refusing to assemble.

"Nineteen thirty-seven," Jayden said from the grass. "That's before my grandma was born. He figured out what every cell in my body is doing right now, and nobody had told him it was happening."

"Nobody had told my cells either," Giovanni said, and for a moment they laughed, but the laughter had an odd weight to it, and Daniel found he wasn't really laughing. He was looking at his own forearm, thinking about trillions of mitochondria, his mother's and his father's and somehow, distantly, strangers', all turning glucose into the currency of his thinking about them.

"Okay, focus," he said, because the feeling was too large for a Tuesday. "Glycolysis first. Two ATP, two pyruvate. Then pyruvate to the mitochondria." He laid the cards in a line down the picnic table, then bent the line into a loop. "Then it's not a line at all. It goes around. Citrate, then the other molecules, then back to the start."

"That's the weird part," Giovanni said. "It's not a path. It's a wheel. Nothing ends."

"And Krebs drew the wheel," Daniel said slowly. "Johnson helped draw the wheel. And the wheel got one name on it." He was aware, even as he said it, that he didn't know the whole story, why the name settled the way it did, whether it settled fairly. The uncertainty sat in him like a stone in a shoe.

Ms. Haddad had told them last week, when Daniel stayed after class to ask about the exam, that she didn't grade on whether you found biology beautiful. She had said it with a dryness that was almost kind. But standing in her classroom doorway, he had asked a peevish question about why they had to memorize all the intermediate compounds, and she had answered, "Because the intermediates are where the ATP comes from," and walked off with a gravitas that made him feel small and curious at the same time. He hadn't liked that feeling. Now, in the backyard, he recognized it again, and this time he let it stay.

"Deal me in," Jayden said, sitting up, grass in his hair. He took a handful of cards and shuffled them badly. "Quiz me on the cycle. And when you say Krebs, I'm going to think of the guy who found out my cells were doing something before he was born to find it out."

"You'll get it wrong if you think like that," Giovanni said.

"No, I'll get it right and think like that at the same time. Those aren't opposites."

Daniel looked at the loop of cards on the table, the wheel that turned glucose into motion and thought, named for one man and built, somehow, by more. He didn't know yet what he believed about naming, or about the parts of knowledge that go unrecorded. He knew the cycle. He turned the first card over.

"Citrate," he said. "Start there."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
The registration page asked for her name twice, once in regular letters and once in capitals, as though the second version were more official, more truly her. Nicole typed it, deleted it, and typed it again, because in four months she would be eighteen, and this was the year she meant to vote. Her mother had never registered, a fact she'd only learned last spring, when her mother said it the way you admit you never learned to swim. Down the hall, the printer ground through her father's tax forms, indifferent.

The problem was not the registration. The problem was the sample ballot she'd pulled up, a local school board election with six names and no party labels, and Nicole knew exactly one of them. She'd come to the desk with a plan: read everything, decide like a juror, be the kind of voter her civics teacher, Ms. Koné, had described as an obligation rather than a right. But the candidate statements were beige paragraphs about fiscal responsibility and "putting students first," interchangeable as keys on a ring, and she'd been sitting for forty minutes with her chin on her wrist.

Her phone lit up with a message from Emerson: still pretending you'll research all six? She typed back that she was, that some things deserved actual thought, and Emerson replied with a photo. It was Emerson's aunt in Chennai, grinning outside a polling station, holding up her right index finger for the camera. The finger was stained a deep bruised purple from the nail to the first knuckle.

What's on her hand, Nicole typed, and while she waited she scrolled, the trackpad slick under her fingertips, until she found it: indelible ink, silver nitrate, used since India's 1962 general election so no one can vote twice. "It doesn't wash off," Emerson wrote. "She wears it for days. She's proud of it, like a badge." Nicole looked at the woman's raised finger, at the purple that would outlast the day itself, and felt something she couldn't immediately name, a small ache of envy for a mark you could show.

She messaged Nathanael, who was also turning eighteen and who had strong opinions delivered entirely in lowercase. he said one of the candidates, the one Nicole recognized, had spoken at a rally last fall and spent the whole speech excoriating the teachers' union, calling them parasites. Nicole had been at that rally with her mother. She remembered it differently, remembered the candidate being angry but precise, and she said so. everyone remembers it the way they already believe, Nathanael wrote back, which Nicole privately thought was the kind of line people used to end arguments they were losing.

She opened two windows side by side: the candidate's voting record, and the only endorsement she trusted, from Ms. Koné, who had once told the class that good policy is autochthonous, that it grows out of the actual soil of a place, its budget, its buses, its particular shortages, and cannot be transplanted from somewhere trendier. Nicole had written the word in her notebook without understanding it until now, reading the school district's overcrowding numbers, its one social worker for eleven hundred students. The zeitgeist, she knew, favored whoever was loudest, and the loudest candidate had the most signs on her street, and Emerson was voting for him because the signs were everywhere, and this, Nicole realized, was exactly how her mother had ended up never voting at all: the noise blurred until it seemed none of it was real.

She read until eleven, made her list, ranked the six, and felt the ranking settle in her like a stone dropping through water. Then she thought about Emerson's aunt holding up her stained finger, and she understood that the mark mattered more than the choice, that showing up was itself the argument, and she understood too that this was only partly comforting, because she was still choosing among strangers, still translating six beige paragraphs into a guess. She could hold both of those truths without either one canceling the other. That felt adult, and also like a loss, the loss of being certain.

Her father passed the door on his way to bed and paused at the glow of her screen. "Still awake?"

"Registering to vote," she said. "It's done. It took an hour."

He stood in the doorway a moment, the hall light behind him. "Your grandmother would have liked that." Then he went on down the hall, and Nicole turned back to her ballot, to the six names glowing in the dark, and dragged the page into a folder she named, after a minute, first time.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer.
story:
Laura had decided, on the bus to camp, that she was not going to be nervous, which was why her hands were shaking, because they were cold from the air conditioning. The art seminar met in a pavilion that smelled of pine sap and bug spray, and Ms. Nur had taped a print of a Frida Kahlo painting above the chalkboard on the first day, before anyone had even unpacked.

"You'll each present a formal critique on Friday," Ms. Nur said. "Colour, composition, symbolism. Not biography, not feelings. Evidence."

Laura had wanted to seem impressive, so she had chosen The Broken Column without looking at it for longer than three seconds. This was, she would later admit to almost no one, a mistake. The painting showed Kahlo standing in a cracked desert landscape, a split Ionic column where her spine should be, and nails driven into her face and body, dozens of them, while tears ran down her cheeks. And yet she looked straight at the viewer. Laura had set her phone face-down on the picnic table and gone to find water she did not need.

Sawyer was at the water pump, filling a bottle with the focus of someone deferring a chore. "You picked the hard one," Sawyer said. "Louis-Felix picked a still life with fruit. Fruit doesn't stare at you."

"It doesn't stare," Laura said. "It's paint."

"Okay," said Sawyer, in the tone of someone agreeing to end a conversation rather than win it, which was more irritating than argument. Laura went back to the pavilion and sat with her notebook and her cold hands and wrote "FORMAL ANALYSIS" at the top of a page, then, after a moment, "not biography," because that was the rule and she was good at rules.

The trouble was that she had prepared to talk about palette and composition, and she could do that, she could do it in her sleep. The vertical of the broken column dividing the torso, the horizontal seams of the cloth, the muted greens and browns of the landscape against the pale skin, the surgical corset binding the reds to the greys. She had a whole paragraph. But every time she looked at the print, she felt the painting looking back, and she could not find a formal term for that, and it began to seem like the whole critique hinged on it. She tried telling herself she was being dramatic. She was, if she was honest, given to that, though she rarely was.

Louis-Felix found her on Thursday night on the dock, where she had gone to experience what she privately called atmosphere and what was probably just ennui, the flat grey hours after dinner when the lake stopped being pretty and started being a lake. "Sawyer says you're revising," he said, sitting down without invitation, which was his way. "Ms. Nur says that's allowed until the deadline. Also she says your first draft was, quote, competent but evasive."

"It was formal."

"It was a list," Louis-Felix said. "You described the nails and the tears and the column like you were reading an inventory. You never once said why she's looking at you like that."

"She's not looking at me. There's no me. It's a painting."

Louis-Felix shrugged. "Then say that in your critique. Say the nails pierce her face and her body, and the tears run down her cheeks, and she still looks straight at the viewer, and then say what you think it does. If you can't, say you can't. That's a position too." He flicked a pebble into the water. "My still life has a melon. I have no such problems."

Laura laughed despite herself, and then did not sleep well, and in the morning she wrote a new draft in the mess hall while a counsellor tried to malign the oatmeal to anyone who would listen, calling it glue, calling it war crime, calling it a reason to transfer camps. She wrote: the composition is vertical and divided; the palette is dry and restrained; the symbolism is Catholic and classical and surgical; and the eyes, which I keep trying to avoid, refuse to let me. She wrote that the discomfort of meeting the painted gaze was not a flaw in the viewer but a function of the design, that the tears and the stare worked against each other on purpose, though she could not prove the purpose, only the effect. She crossed out the last clause, then wrote it again.

On Friday she stood under the print with her index card, and her hands were cold again, which she attributed to the pavilion. She spoke about the column and the corset and the nailed skin, and then she said the hard part. "The tears run down her cheeks, and she looks straight at the viewer, and the critique I want to give is that I keep wanting to look away and the painting won't let me. I think that's the strongest thing in it. I can't fully defend that with formal evidence, so I'm marking it as my own judgment, not a conclusion."

Ms. Nur was quiet for a second, which Laura initially interpreted as disaster. "That's the distinction most first-year art historians never learn to make," she said. "Some of them never do. They get doctrinaire about one method and stop seeing the painting at all."

Afterward Sawyer found her by the pumps. "That was good. Weird, but good."

"It was honest," Laura said, and heard how much she wanted that to be the end of it, the medal, the tidy close. But she was already remembering the draft in her bag, the crossed-out clause, the three seconds she had spent choosing a painting she hadn't really looked at, and the whole week of looking away.

"Louis-Felix wants to know if you'll help him with his melon," Sawyer said. "He says it's symbolic of something and he can't figure out what."

Laura capped her pen. "Tell him the melon is symbolic of choosing the easy painting."

"He already knows that. He says that's the symbolism."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
The car had been loaded since dawn, and Christopher sat in the back seat with a shoebox of things he had refused to let his father pack: three mixtapes, a dented harmonica, a folded map of Riverside with Micheal's house circled in green marker. The map was four years old. Micheal and Sandrine had stood in the driveway until the garage door opened behind them, and Micheal had knocked twice on the roof of the car, the way you knock on wood, and Sandrine had said nothing at all, which was worse.

"Two hundred miles," his father said, watching the mirror more than the road. "You'll be there by lunch."

Christopher did the math against his knee. Two hundred miles, then a new school on Monday, then a bedroom with no marks on the doorframe where his height had been measured. Sandrine had given him a notebook at the going-away party, spiral-bound, spartan, plain brown cover, and inside the front flap she had written a sentence he'd read eleven times: Studies say it takes about 90 hours together to turn a casual friend into a real friend. Underneath she'd added, that's from a 2018 study, Jeffrey Hall, look it up. He'd looked it up on his phone in the driveway, one bar of signal, and the numbers held. Ninety hours. He'd thought she was being dramatic.

"Sandrine thinks friendship is arithmetic," he said to the window.

His mother turned around in her seat. "What was that?"

"Nothing. She read this thing. A researcher figured out how long it takes to make a friend. Ninety hours."

"Ninety hours of what?"

"Of being together. Going from casual to actual friend." He hadn't meant to say it out loud, and now it sat in the car like a third passenger.

His father tapped the wheel. "Family's different. Consanguinity, all that. Blood doesn't keep a log."

Christopher let it go. Blood doesn't keep a log, but blood also doesn't choose, which was the whole point Sandrine had been circling for months without saying it: Micheal and he had chosen each other in fourth grade over a broken controller, and every hour after that had been a choice, and now the choosing was being done for him by a job offer and a leased house in a town he'd never heard of. He counted backward in his notebook, mile markers ticking past. Lunches, roughly forty minutes. Saturdays, call it six hours. He wrote the numbers down and stopped, because the total was obscene, hundreds of hours spent on a person, thousands, and it hadn't felt like spending. That was the part the study couldn't measure.

At the halfway rest stop his mother took over the driver's seat and his father went in for coffee, and for a while she watched Christopher in the mirror while he thought she was asleep behind his sunglasses. She had watched him lose things before, the dog at nine, the grandfather at twelve, and each time he had gone quiet and then, without announcement, resuscitated himself, joining something, showing up somewhere, inventing a version of himself that hadn't been hurt. She suspected the notebook was that. She suspected the notebook was also a wall.

"You could call him tonight," she said.

"I will."

"From the new house. The internet gets set up Thursday."

"I said I will."

She let three miles pass. "You know Sandrine called me last week. While you were at practice." She kept her eyes on the road. "She wanted to know if you'd have your own room. I asked why, and she said, so he has somewhere for us to stay when we visit. She'd already worked out the bus route."

Christopher's pen stopped. He looked at the notebook, at his columns of hours, and felt something loosen that he didn't want loosened. He had been treating the move like a border crossing, and Sandrine had been treating it like a longer commute.

"Eighty hours by bus?" he said.

"Something like that."

He turned to a fresh page and started a different column. If Micheal came for a weekend, that was maybe thirty hours. If he went back for a week in summer, more. It wasn't the same as Saturdays, but the study hadn't said the hours had to be consecutive, or in one town, or before you were sixteen. He was still working when his phone buzzed against his thigh.

Micheal had sent a photo of Sandrine's notebook, the twin of his own, opened to a page headed with Christopher's name and a running tally that had been started months ago, before anyone said the word moving. Beside it Micheal had written: we're at like 4000, loser. you do the rest of the math.

Christopher typed a reply, deleted it, typed another, and in the front seat his mother watched the highway signs count down toward a town she'd only seen in photographs, while behind her, very quietly, her son began to laugh.

"One more thing," his father said, settling back in with his coffee. "The new place. I signed you up for something. Robotics club, Tuesday nights. Mr. Banerjee runs it, he's my department head's husband."

"Nine Tuesdays," Christopher said, almost to himself, already counting.

"Nine what?"

"Nothing. Tuesdays."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Jewish law, the principle of pikuach nefesh holds that saving a human life overrides almost every other commandment, including the rules of the Sabbath.
story:
The community hall smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and the folding chairs had been arranged in a horseshoe for the debate society's first real practice of the year. Alex sat with a photocopy of Exodus 35 spread across his knees, three verses highlighted and no idea what to do with them. The motion for next month's regional round was that an ancient religious rule cannot meaningfully apply to modern life, and Mr. Esposito had drawn his side as the one defending the rule.

"You look like a boy who has been disabused of the idea that debating is easy," Matthieu said, dropping into the next chair and peeling an orange.

"I look like a boy with three verses and a losing case." Alex turned the page over as though the back might help. "Everyone on the other side will talk about medicine, emergencies, ambulances. Meanwhile I'm standing there quoting 'you shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the Sabbath day.'"

Milla arrived late, her coat still on, and set down her phone with the timer already running. "Twenty minutes until Esposito makes us do an exhibition round. What have we got?"

Alex told her: the rule, the motion, the problem. The rule said no work on the Sabbath, not even fire, and modern life was made of work and fire and engines. He had planned to argue that the rule created rest, that rest was a value modern people had lost, and he could hear already how the opposing speakers would flatten it with one story about a car and a hospital.

Milla suggested the straw man approach: define "modern life" so narrowly that nothing counted. Matthieu suggested arguing that the rule had never applied to nonbelievers, which Alex pointed out was giving away the motion entirely. The timer counted down on the phone's cracked screen.

Then, while Matthieu argued that an ancient rule was like an allotrope of carbon, the same substance arranged differently in a different century, Alex flipped back to the packet Mr. Esposito had photocopied from a reference shelf, a collection of legal discussions he had skimmed the night before and mostly ignored. Near the bottom of one page, in a passage about physicians, a phrase appeared twice, and he stopped on it.

"Milla. Listen to this." He read aloud, awkward with the transliteration. "The physician may violate the Sabbath when a life is in danger, because of pikuach nefesh."

"What's that mean?"

"It's the principle of saving a life," Alex said, reading the line that followed. "Saving a human life overrides almost every other commandment, including the rules of the Sabbath."

The three of them sat with it for a moment. Milla took the packet and read further, lips moving. "So the rule contains its own exception. Like the rule knows."

"Then the ambulance argument doesn't work against us," Alex said, and the idea assembled itself as he spoke, still embryonic but with a shape now. "If the tradition already holds that you drive someone to hospital on the Sabbath, that saving the life comes first, then the rule isn't fighting modern life. It was never the kind of rule the other side is attacking."

Mr. Esposito clapped his hands from the front of the horseshoe. "Exhibition round. Alex, you're opening. Motion stands."

Alex stood behind the little plywood podium and made the case, slower than he wanted, the photocopy shaking slightly in his hand. He quoted the verses about fire. Then he said the phrase, pikuach nefesh, and explained only what the packet had said, that saving a life overrides almost every other commandment, and let it sit.

In the reply, a girl from the other bench stood and did exactly what he had predicted, the ambulance story, the grandmother, the snow. She was good. The room was quiet for her, and Alex watched his argument seem to shrink, because she had built her case as though the exception did not exist, and now the judges would have to choose whose version of the rule was the real one.

He had one minute of rebuttal. He stood up again.

"You told us about the grandmother," he said. "Under this law, driving her is not a violation. It's required." He paused, hearing the limits of what he had: a packet, one phrase, a tradition he did not belong to and had met nine hours ago. "I'm not sure the rule always wins the motion. I'm sure it doesn't lose the way you said."

The girl tilted her head, and Mr. Esposito wrote something on his clipboard without looking up.

"Point of information," the girl said, raising her pen. "So what else does it override?"

"I don't know yet," Alex said, and sat down.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
The library smelled of radiator dust and old glue, and Austin had forty minutes before Ms. Tan called him to the front table for his oral. The article lay flat between his elbows, three paragraphs of Spanish about a flood, printed from a website Kale had found the night before. Austin could read most of it. What he could not do yet was say it back in his own words, out loud, without his voice going thin.

Kale sat across from him with the same article, pencil tapping. "I already did mine last period," he said. "Summarized it in like four sentences. Easy."

"What did you say it was about?"

"Floods in, I said Colombia. Some town got hit, they evacuated people." Kale shrugged, and the shrug had something in it Austin couldn't read, a small hesitation that he filed away because he had his own problems.

Mael pulled a chair over without asking, dropped his bag, and leaned in. "You're both wrong, by the way. Kale, you mean Colombia, but check the country. Austin, read the first line again. Aloud."

Austin read it. A city name, then a date, then a comma, and only after that the sentence began. He had skimmed straight past the opening on his first read, hungry for verbs he recognized. He read it again, slower. The city was not in Colombia. He looked up. "Wait. Where's the dateline?"

"Dateline," Mael said, pointing at it. "That's the dateline."

"That's part of it? I thought it was like a header thing. Decoration."

"It's the city where the story was reported. It sits there before the first sentence. Every news story's got one like that." Mael turned his palm up, as if presenting something obvious that had been sitting between them the whole time.

Austin sat back. His summary, drafted in pencil, said Colombia, because Kale had said Colombia, and because Austin had trusted a friend's memory over his own eyes. He erased it. The tense part was the clock now: twenty-five minutes, and the pencil moved fast, rewriting the opening sentence around the real country, around the real river, and his heartbeat occupied him briefly, the plain physiology of fear, hands damp, pulse in his ears, before he made himself read the whole thing aloud once, quietly, into the shelf of atlases.

"Why'd you even say Colombia?" Austin asked, not looking up.

Kale was quiet long enough that Austin did look up. "Because I said it in my oral. Last period. To Ms. Tan." He said it evenly, but his pencil had stopped. "She didn't correct me or anything. She just wrote something down."

The equanimity of that, the not-knowing whether the mark was already against him, sat on the table between all three of them. Mael offered to go find out, which would have allayed nothing, and Kale said no, don't, which was its own kind of answer. Austin turned back to his page.

Ms. Tan came at the end of the period with her clipboard. She stood over their table for a moment before speaking, and the moment lasted too long. "Austin, you're first," she said. "Sixty seconds. In Spanish if you can, English if you must."

Austin stood. The summary waited in his head, rebuilt, and the dateline came out first, the way it came in the paper, the city named before anything else, and then the flood, the evacuation, the river. He heard his own voice stay level, which surprised him, and he watched Ms. Tan's pencil and could not tell from her face whether the pencil meant good or bad, and he understood that he would not know today. Kale was next, and Austin took his seat and did not look at him. Kale stood, smoothed the page, and began, "A flood in Colombia," and Austin watched Ms. Tan's pencil pause above the clipboard, hovering, before it came down and wrote something none of them could see.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
Antoine had pictured the food bank in a church basement somewhere, but the notice had said Fairview Seniors' Residence, and so he pushed through the glass doors at ten in the morning with a box of granola bars under one arm and no idea what he was supposed to do with it. A woman in a lanyard pointed him down the hall toward the common room, where folding tables had been arranged in a horseshoe and boxes of pasta, cans of peas, and tubes of baby cereal waited in uneven stacks. Savana was already there, cutting open a carton with a key, and beside her a thin old man in a cardigan sat in an armchair as though supervising a parade.

"You're the fourth one," Savana said. "Kayden's in the washroom and Ms. Demir went to get tape. Take the granola bars to that end."

The old man introduced himself as Harold, though Antoine had not asked, and explained that he had lived at Fairview for six years and that the food bank ran out of the common room on the second Saturday of every month because the residence had the only elevator on the street. "I sit here so people don't feel like they're stealing," he said. "A lady comes for a hamper, she sees a man my age watching, she thinks, well, someone official must be in charge." He seemed pleased with this arrangement. Antoine asked whether he was in charge, and Harold said that he was in charge of sitting, which was a skill like any other.

The work turned out to be simple and repetitive: read the slip, fill the hamper. A slip marked a family of four got two of everything plus whatever special items were circled. Antoine noticed, by the third slip, that the circled items were almost always the same: baby food, rice cereal, the small applesauce cups, juice boxes, sometimes diapers. He began setting those aside in a separate row so he wouldn't have to keep hunting for them. Savana watched him do it and nodded as though he'd passed some quiet test.

"Ms. Demir told me a number last week," she said, taping a box shut. "One-third. Kids, I mean. Children made up about a third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. It's from the HungerCount report, Food Banks Canada does it." She said it the way she said most things, flat and quick, as if the fact were heavy and she wanted to set it down between them and step back. "That's why we're always out of the apple stuff."

Antoine kept packing, but the number followed him down the row of boxes. He had expected the hampers to be for old people, or for the kind of adults he imagined waiting outside shelters, and the picture in his head had not included anyone small enough for rice cereal. He thought of his chemistry teacher's habit of ionizing a gas to reveal its hidden lines, making the invisible show itself as colour, and he felt the statistic do something like that to the room: the boxes were the same boxes, the cans the same cans, and yet he could suddenly see who the cans were for.

A woman arrived at eleven with a stroller and a boy of maybe five who pressed his face to the fish tank near the window. Ms. Demir took her slip, and Antoine filled the hamper: pasta, sauce, oats, peanut butter, a jar of baby food, two juice boxes, the applesauce. Harold stood up from his armchair, which he had not done all morning, and dug a plastic bag out of the pocket of his cardigan. Inside were a handful of wrapped candies he had evidently been saving. He crouched, with some trouble, and held one out to the boy. "For after lunch," he said. "Not before, and don't tell your mother I said that." The boy took it with both hands.

When the woman had gone, Harold lowered himself back into the chair and looked at the fish tank as though nothing had happened. Antoine found that he wanted to say something but couldn't find a shape for it. He believed, in a general way, that volunteering was good, the way he believed exercise was good, and he had come that morning mostly so the line on his scholarship form would not be blank. That felt smaller now than it had at breakfast, though he couldn't have said whether smaller meant worse or just different. And there was a further question he couldn't shake: if a third of the visits were children, then somewhere there was a machine, a country, a set of choices that kept producing that number, and a Saturday of hampers touched the number without moving it. He held both thoughts at once, the worth of the morning and its limits, and did not try to collapse one into the other.

Savana broke in on this by asking what he was staring at. "Nothing," he said. "The applesauce row. It's half gone already."

"Mercurial crowd," Kayden said, returning from the washroom and drying his hands on his jeans. "Some Saturdays we're drowning in tomato soup, other days it's like a plague came through. You can't predict it." He picked up the last slip of the morning and read it twice. "Family of five," he said, and held it out to Antoine. "You do the math on the cereal. I still don't know how many cans of peas is too many."

"How many is too many?" Antoine asked.

"There's no such thing," Kayden said, "according to Ms. Demir. She says probity in food banking means you never guess, you weigh everything and you write it down." He grinned. "I just count."

Antoine filled the hamper, and when he reached for the baby cereal he found the row empty. He stood there a moment, holding a slip with three circles on it, and then walked over to Ms. Demir at the sign-in table and asked, quietly, what he was supposed to do now.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Accounting profit subtracts only money actually paid out, while economic profit also subtracts implicit costs such as the owner's time and the next-best use of their money.
story:
The vending machine outside the economics room took Elijah's dollar and gave nothing back, which felt like an omen, so he leaned against the wall and waited for Katia, who was always the last one out because she packed her laptop with the care of someone handling evidence. She was already talking before the door swung shut behind her. Sixty-three dollars of profit this month, she said, thumbing through the screens of her sticker shop, forty customers, repeat buyers, an actual spreadsheet. "Look at this row. Revenue minus supplies minus shipping. That's profit."

Elijah walked with her down the hall, past the trophy case, and asked the question that had been sitting in him since Tuesday. "What about your hours?" Katia stopped at the water fountain. She designed each sticker herself, printed test batches, sealed the mailers at her kitchen table, answered messages at midnight. He had watched her decline Gage's pickup game on Thursday for it, and again on Saturday, and he had started keeping a private tally without meaning to, the way you count something you are quietly losing. "If you paid yourself even minimum wage for all that," he said, "would the sixty-three survive?"

She drank water and didn't answer, which was its own answer. Gage caught up with them at the corner by the gym, bouncing a ball he had taken from the equipment rack without asking, calling the coach a despot in a tone that was half a joke and half not, because the man really did ration the good balls like ammunition. Gage said the shop sounded like a scam if it couldn't pay its own owner. Katia said that was doctrinaire, that not everything worth doing pays you, and Gage said that was exactly what a person losing money would say, and both of them looked at Elijah as if he were the referee.

He wasn't ready to be the referee. In class that morning, Ms. Yamamoto had written two columns on the board, and Elijah had copied them without understanding, and only now, holding Katia's phone in the stairwell while she tied her shoe, did the columns rearrange themselves in his head. "Okay," he said slowly. "There's two kinds of profit. Accounting profit subtracts only money you actually paid out. Supplies, shipping, fees. You've got sixty-three of that. But economic profit also subtracts the implicit stuff. Your time. The next-best use of your money, like what your printer fund could have earned anywhere else. Once you count those, you might be underwater." He handed the phone back. "You're not lying about making money. You're just measuring it one way."

Katia took the phone and scrolled her spreadsheet in silence, and Elijah watched her subtract, tentatively, in her head, an hour here, an hour there, the Friday nights, the Sunday afternoons. Her face did the thing faces do when arithmetic turns personal. "It's negative," she said finally. "Like, deeply negative." Gage, who had been spinning the ball on one finger, stopped spinning it. The stairwell was loud with the change of classes, doors slamming somewhere below, and the three of them stood in that noise holding three different versions of the same girl's small business.

But Elijah wasn't finished, because the same logic kept moving, and it did not stop at Katia's spreadsheet. He had turned down the fall play for this schedule, for the study blocks, for the transcript he'd been told would underwrite everything after June, and if someone charged his own hours against that choice, counted what the stage and the Thursday pickup games and one unremarkable Saturday with friends were worth, he could not say his own profit was positive either. He said as much to the stairwell, half to himself. "I think I'm running your shop." Katia frowned. Gage laughed, once, and then didn't.

Katia announced she would keep the shop anyway. She would make a real wage for herself out of it someday, she said, raise prices, batch the printing, stop answering messages at midnight, and in the meantime the negative number was the tuition. Gage called that romantic. She called him an accountant. She smiled when she said it, though, and took the ball from him and spun it once, badly, and handed it back, and the bell rang and pulled them down the stairwell in separate directions.

At the bottom, Elijah stopped at the vending machine again and fed it another dollar, and this time the machine thought about it and returned the coin, the exact coin, with a clunk. He stood there holding his own money, unchanged, in his open palm.

"Still thirsty?" Katia called from the door.

"Yeah," he said, and pocketed it.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The cuff hissed twice before it gave up, and the number on the little screen made Tyler's father go quiet in a way Tyler had learned to read before he could read anything else. 138 over 88, the display said, blinking. His father pressed the button again, as though the machine might change its mind.

"It's for my health project," Tyler said, which was only partly true. Ms. Gauthier had assigned the class a topic each, and his was hypertension, and part of the assignment was to teach the concept to somebody at home. But the cuff was in the closet because his father had been told to keep an eye on things, and nobody in the house had been looking.

He texted Melanie, who had the same assignment and had already been to the pharmacy to use their machine on herself three times. She sent back a photo of a page from her notes. Under the 2017 guideline, she'd written, normal for adults is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. He sat on the kitchen floor with the phone between his knees and stared at it. Systolic was the top number; that much he'd picked up. So 138 was above 120, and 88 was above 80, and neither of those was normal, and his father was in the living room pretending to watch golf.

"Is that bad?" his father called, because fathers could hear the silence of a son reading something twice.

"It's not normal," Tyler said carefully. "Normal's under 120 over 80. That's the guideline." He did not say the word bad. He was beginning to understand that in this house the two words had been used interchangeably for years, and that part of what he was learning was to disabuse everyone, himself included, of the idea that a number on a screen was a verdict.

He called Melanie back that evening and they argued for twenty minutes, the way they did, which was the way some people collaborated. She thought the whole assignment was a trap, that telling people their numbers would just make them anxious and anxious people eat worse. Tyler thought people deserved to know the scale of the thing. "You can't make restitution to somebody's heart," Melanie said, "for years of drive-through, by handing them a pamphlet." He wrote that down, because it was better than anything in his notes, and then disagreed with it, and then half-agreed, and they hung up without settling anything, which was usual.

The part Ms. Gauthier wanted, the explaining part, was what kept him up. He kept wanting to say that diet and exercise lower blood pressure, full stop, like a law of physics, and the sources kept refusing to say it that simply. They talked about patterns, about averages across populations, about sodium and activity and weeks and months, never about one specific man on one specific couch. His father, meanwhile, had started doing something Tyler had not asked for and could not have predicted: he walked the block after dinner. Not fast, not far. Once around, past Ms. Gauthier's place, where her roses had gone friable at the edges from the dry summer, petals crumbling under his fingers when he stopped, the way he stopped, to look at them and let the walking count as walking.

On Sunday Tyler set the cuff on the table before dinner. "For the project," he said. "I have to demonstrate."

His father held out his arm without being asked, which was its own kind of answer. The machine hummed, tightened, let go. 128 over 84. Tyler copied it into his notebook, and his father leaned sideways to see, and neither of them said what they were both doing, which was comparing.

"That's different," his father said.

"It's one reading," Tyler said. "You can't tell anything from one reading. The guideline's about where you sit over time, not one afternoon." This was the honest version, the one the sources kept circling: the number told you where the line was, and not what would happen next, and not who would cross back over it, or when. He believed the walking mattered. He could not prove it, and he was tired of pretending the difference between believing and proving didn't exist.

Ms. Gauthier had said their grade would rest on the explanation, on whether they could hold two things in mind at once: what the evidence showed, and where the evidence ran out. Tyler shut his notebook and carried the plates to the sink. Through the window he could see his father already at the front walk, stretching one hamstring with his hand on the fence post, in the last of the light.

"Wait up," Tyler called through the screen door, grabbing his jacket.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.
story:
Nathaniel had claimed the corner table at the Blue Line Café with a stack of index cards, a borrowed style manual, and the particular malaise of a boy three days from a deadline. His paper was supposed to argue something, actually argue it, with footnotes and a bibliography in proper form, and so far his strongest claim was that fireflies sync their flashes, which he had copied word for word from a library book onto a card marked, optimistically, "my thinking."

Loick slid into the opposite chair uninvited, holding a hot chocolate the size of a small aquarium. "Tell me you're not doing the firefly paper."

"It's a legitimate topic."

"It's a legitimate topic for a nine-year-old. Also, I need a favor. Saturday. My cousin's band, they're short a door person, you just take the money and look tired. I'll owe you."

"I have a deadline."

"You always have a deadline. Your whole personality is deadlines." Loick leaned over and plucked a card from the stack. "This isn't even writing. This is just copying."

"That's what research is. You find facts, you put them in."

Loick read the card aloud in a documentary-voiceover baritone, clearly enjoying himself. "Fireflies of certain species flash in synchrony, an emergent behavior with no conductor." He looked up. "Emergent behavior with no conductor. Did you write that?"

Nathaniel took the card back. "The book wrote that. But here's the fix, watch." He crossed out the sentence and rewrote it below: some fireflies all blink at the same time, and no single one is in charge. "There. My own words now. No citation needed, because I didn't copy it."

Loick squinted at the card, then at Nathaniel, then at his hot chocolate as if it might arbitrate. "That feels legal but wrong. Like a loophole in a board game."

"It's paraphrasing. That's the whole point of paraphrasing."

At the counter, Mr. García was waiting for a cappuccino, still in his bike helmet, and Nathaniel felt the specific dread of being observed in the act of academic sin by the one adult in town who taught tenth-grade history. Mr. García waved. He was not, technically, Nathaniel's teacher this year, which made him safe in the way of off-duty police officers.

"Mr. García," Nathaniel called, because the dread had to be resolved or it would ruin the afternoon. "Hypothetical. If you put someone's idea in your own words, do you still cite it?"

Mr. García carried his cup over, considered the index cards the way a man considers weather, and said only, "Plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording." Then he wished them luck with the fireflies and went back to the counter, where he began to pontificate to the cashier about the correct thickness of milk foam, a subject on which he appeared to have strong and unshareable convictions.

Nathaniel sat with that sentence for a moment. It rearranged something. The card in his hand, with its crossed-out source and its breezy rewrite, was not fixed; it was the problem wearing a disguise. He turned it over and wrote the book's name and page in the corner, small and neat, the way the style manual showed.

"So the paraphrase counts," Loick said slowly. "The idea is the thing. The words were never the crime."

"The words were never the crime," Nathaniel agreed, and felt the pleasure of a rule understood rather than memorized, which was new enough to be almost alarming. He flipped through the rest of his cards and found four more disguises, sentences laundered into casual language and set loose without credit. He began marking them, and the stack, which had looked finished an hour ago, revealed itself as barely started.

"About Saturday," Loick said, and there was something careful in his voice now, a looseness that had been arranged. "The real reason I need you is my cousin said if I bring someone reliable, he'll let me open for them next time. Me. With my trumpet. In front of people."

Nathaniel looked up. Loick was stirring his hot chocolate with great concentration, as though the marshmallows had opinions.

"I'll do it," Nathaniel said, "if you read my first paragraph and tell me honestly if it sounds like a person wrote it or a very ambitious firefly."

Loick held out his hand across the index cards. "Deal. But if it's bad, I'm going to say it's good, because I need Saturday."

"That's a footnote waiting to happen."

"Then cite me."

Nathaniel laughed, uncapped his pen, and wrote the citation in the corner of the last card.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 1942 sociologist Robert K. Merton named 'organized skepticism' as a norm of science: claims must survive critical scrutiny by the community before they are accepted.
story:
The printout trembled a little in Peyton's hand, which annoyed her, because she had promised herself it would not. Her science fair project, forty bean seedlings grown under identical conditions except for the variable, had produced a clean result, and for three days the poster board had hung in the gymnasium like a small flag she had planted. Then Victor had leaned in during lunch, tapped the graph, and asked whether she'd grown a second batch. Then Jada had asked if she'd mixed up the labels on any of the pots, just once, just possibly. Then a boy from another homeroom had asked who had checked her work, and Peyton had heard herself say, in a voice she didn't love, "I checked it."

She took her irritation to the public library after school, because that was where she went when she needed to be somewhere that expected quiet. Ms. Weiss was at the reference desk transcribing titles from a donation box into a ledger, since the library's penurious budget meant every free book had to be counted twice. She looked up when Peyton dumped her binder on the desk.

"I need proof that my project counts," Peyton said. "Something I can quote. Something that says one careful experiment is enough."

Ms. Weiss didn't answer right away. She finished the line she was writing, capped her pen, and turned the ledger to a blank page. "What you probably want is a quote about how science gets accepted. Not whether your beans grew. Whether anyone has to believe you."

They went into the stacks together, past the study tables where Jada sat with a stack of books about the justice system, highlighting every appearance of the word recidivism for her own project, the one about whether prison education programs lowered the rate at which people returned. Jada waved without looking up. Peyton felt a small pinch of guilt about the lunch table, about the way she'd closed her binder like a door.

The sociology section was one shelf, half of it water-damaged. Ms. Weiss pulled a thick green book and set it on the cart, then left Peyton alone with it, which Peyton understood was deliberate. She read the index, found the page, and read it twice. In 1942, a sociologist named Robert K. Merton had written about the norms of science, and one of them he had called organized skepticism. Claims, the passage said, had to survive the critical scrutiny of the community before they were accepted. Not one reviewer. Not the experimenter herself. The community. Peyton sat back on her heels between the shelves and let the unfairness of it wash over her, and then, slower, the fairness.

She found Jada at the study table and sat down across from her.

"Did you know that in 1942 a sociologist named Robert K. Merton named organized skepticism as a norm of science?" Peyton said. "Claims have to survive critical scrutiny by the community before they're accepted. That's what he said."

"So everyone gets doubted, not just you."

"So everyone gets doubted, exactly like me." Peyton turned Jada's highlighter over in her fingers. "Which means Victor wasn't being a jerk. He was doing the job."

"He thinks he's being a jerk sometimes," Jada said. "He told me he felt bad about lunch. He just couldn't stop wondering about your labels."

Peyton looked down at the table. The library's overhead lights hummed, and somewhere behind them a printer ground through a page. She thought about her forty seedlings, all alive in her mind at once, and about the forty she hadn't grown, the ones that existed only as an absence, and how the difference between those two groups was the difference between a result and an answer. She couldn't decide yet whether she believed her own number. That was the part she hadn't expected to be allowed to say out loud.

Victor was at the door twenty minutes later, still in his soccer jacket, holding his bike helmet by the strap. Jada had texted him. Peyton stood up before she could plan what she'd say.

"I'll grow the second batch," she told him. "Same soil, same shelf, labels in a different color so we can't confuse them. You can mix up which pots are which so even I won't know. You do the blind part."

Victor set the helmet on the nearest table. "I can come Saturday. My dad has extra trays in the garage."

"I'll bring the beans," Peyton said, and she picked up her binder, and they walked out together past the reference desk, where Ms. Weiss was still counting.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
Rosalie had taped the drawing to the kitchen window so she could see it the way a stranger would, and the stranger, she had to admit, would see a hallway with no depth at all. The floor, the ceiling, the lockers she had invented to stand in for the ones at school, all of it lay flat as wrapping paper. Ms. Popescu had written one word at the bottom of the assignment sheet in her slanted red ink, "hallway, convincingly receding," and circled it twice, which was as close as she came to shouting.

She sat down at the table with a fresh pencil and tried again, this time drawing the lines of the ceiling and floor exactly parallel, because parallel lines were honest, weren't they, two rails that never lied about never meeting. The second drawing came out flatter than the first. She pressed her palm against her eyes until she saw grey shapes swim there, and the effort seemed to enervate her rather than sharpen her, her arm heavy on the table, the pencil wobbling.

Her phone buzzed. Lyric had sent a photo of her own attempt, a kitchen with a table that looked like it was falling over sideways, and beneath it, "mine looks like it got hit by a bus, yours?" Rosalie sent back the window photo without comment. For a while they typed in fragments, blaming the paper, blaming the pencils, until Lyric, who was the sort of person who looked things up the way other people tapped their feet, pasted a link and added, "wait, this guy fixed it like six hundred years ago."

The link was about Florence. Rosalie read it twice, one hand still holding her pencil, because the sentence seemed too plain to be the answer. Around 1420 in Florence, a man named Filippo Brunelleschi had demonstrated linear perspective, which was the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface. She said it out loud to the empty kitchen just to hear whether it could be true. "Lines that meet," she said. All this time she had been drawing lines that refused to meet, and the meeting was the whole point.

She took a third sheet and made a small dot in the middle of it with the pencil, almost nothing, a period at the end of a sentence she hadn't written yet. Then she drew the ceiling lines down toward the dot and the floor lines up toward it, and where she had guessed a doorway might go, she made its sides lean inward, politely, like people at a party tilting toward the same conversation. The hallway appeared. It happened in the space of about ninety seconds and it felt less like an achievement than like being let in on something that had been going on behind her back her whole life.

She called Lyric instead of texting. "Put a dot on the paper," she said. "Just a dot, right in the middle. Then make everything go toward it." There was silence on the line, the scratchy silence of someone drawing fast, and then Lyric made a sound into the phone that was not quite a word, closer to phonetics than language, a vowel of pure astonishment. "It goes back," Lyric said. "Rosalie, it goes back into the paper."

They stayed on the phone while they worked, mostly not talking. Rosalie darkened the lockers nearest to her, the invented ones, and let the far ones pale, though she wasn't sure whether that was part of the rule or just something that looked right, and she was honest enough with herself to mark that question and leave it open. She was equally unsure about the dot itself, whether it belonged where she had put it or lower, where a person's eye would actually rest. The answer in the book had seemed complete, and yet here it was splitting into smaller questions the moment she touched it, which was either frustrating or the most interesting thing that had happened all week.

When the hallway was finished she held it at arm's length, then closer, then at arm's length again. It receded. It convincingly receded, if she could trust her own eyes, and her own eyes had been wrong about parallel lines for two days, so their verdict was at best equivocal. She photographed it and sent it to Ms. Popescu anyway, because a teacher who circled things twice deserved to see the hallway the same night rather than waiting for Monday. Then she took the first flat drawing down from the window and looked at it one more time before turning it over. She left the second one face up on the counter, lines forever parallel, going nowhere together, and got out a clean sheet to see what the dot would do to a street.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 2018 economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and old sweat, and Jordan had spent most of Tuesday's practice missing. Twelve shots, three makes. Coach kept him in anyway, which felt worse than being benched, because after every miss the coach said the same word: "Again."

In the locker room afterward, Viviane was waiting with her laptop open on the bench. She didn't play; she kept stats for the team because Ms. Malik had suggested it would look good on a college application, and because Viviane liked arguments more than she liked running. "You're shooting thirty-one percent from three this month," she said. "Last month you shot forty-four. I looked it up."

"So I'm cold."

"That's what the coach says. He told Shaun on Friday that streaks aren't real, that a made shot doesn't change the odds of the next one. He said a study proved it in 1985." She turned the laptop toward him. "Except some economists went back and checked."

Jordan sat down beside her, still in his damp jersey. The screen showed a paper dense with notation he couldn't parse, so he read the abstract out loud in pieces. In 2018, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed the 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias, and found evidence of streak shooting in the same data that the old study had used to deny it.
