He read that sentence twice. "The same data," he said. "They didn't even need new numbers?"

"Same data," Viviane said. "The original study was just wrong about how you're supposed to count."

Jordan wanted to believe her. He wanted it so much that he distrusted the wanting, because the wish and the evidence had arrived at the same moment, and he'd been raised, mostly by his mother, to be suspicious of convenient conclusions. That night he lay on his bed with his phone on his chest and thought about the coach, a man whose rectitude on this subject had the hardness of something worn smooth by repetition. The coach was not stupid. He had played four years of college ball. But he had also said, more than once, that feelings didn't belong in basketball, and Jordan was beginning to wonder whether that was a fact or a preference dressed up as one.

Thursday, Jordan got to the gym early. The floor was empty except for Shaun, who was lying on the bleachers being blase about a chemistry test he had probably not studied for. Jordan took a ball from the rack and started at the free-throw line. He made one, then another, then two more, and he felt something loosen in his shoulders that he had been pretending not to notice for three weeks. He missed the fifth. He made the sixth. He tried to watch himself the way Viviane would watch him, counting without hoping, and he found he couldn't fully do both at once. The counting and the feeling kept elbowing each other.

"You're in a groove," Shaun called from the bleachers, not looking up from his phone.

"I don't know what I'm in," Jordan said. He bounced the ball once, hard, and listened to it come back up.

At Friday's practice he told the coach, quietly, during a water break, about the two economists and the bias and the same data. The coach's face did the thing faces do when a belief is asked to move and refuses. "Economists," he said, as if the word settled it. "Numbers don't know the game." Jordan didn't argue. He'd decided over two days of turning it over that he couldn't claim streaks were certainly real either, that all he could honestly hold was that the old certainty was gone, that the door had been reopened by people who had bothered to recount. That position felt smaller and more durable than either the coach's no or Shaun's yes.

Ms. Malik, who had come to watch the last twenty minutes from the doorway, caught him afterward. "Viviane told me you were reading probability papers," she said. "For basketball."

"It started as basketball," Jordan said. "I'm not sure that's all it is now."

The coach called the team back onto the floor for scrimmages before she could answer. Jordan took his position at the top of the key, ball in his hands, and for a second he let himself feel what he was no longer allowed to simply assume. Then Viviane, on the sideline with her clipboard, tapped her pen twice against her knee, and he drove to the basket.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The upright piano in Grandma Dot's front room had been a coffee table, a repository for unopened mail, and, for one summer, a home for a parakeet named Neil, but it had never once, in Ryan's sixteen years, been a piano. He lifted the lid anyway, because he'd told Madyson he would, and Madyson had a way of asking about things later, casually, at lunch, that made lying inadvisable.

"Eighty-eight," he said out loud, before he had thought about it.

"What?" Madyson said. She was sprawled on Grandma Dot's sofa with her phone held above her face, which was how she did everything, including apparently accompanying him on this errand.

"The keys. There are eighty-eight. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black." He had counted them while waiting for his lesson at Ms. Morningstar's studio last Tuesday, because the lesson was forty minutes of scales and the wall clock was slow, and there was nothing else to do. He had counted white keys first, then black, then both, to make sure arithmetic still worked in a room that smelled like lavender and correction.

Madyson sat up. "You counted the keys on a piano."

"I was bored."

"You were bored and you counted them and now you're counting my grandmother's."

"Our grandmother's," Ryan said, which was technically true twice a week and had never mattered until now. Grandma Dot had gone into the home in March, and the house was being emptied by Saturday, and the piano was the one thing nobody wanted. His mother said it wasn't worth moving. His uncle said it wasn't worth anything at all. Madyson had said, on the drive over, that they couldn't just let it go to the curb like a couch, and Ryan had agreed before he understood he was volunteering.

The middle C, when he pressed it, made a sound like a walnut cracking. The D next to it said nothing at all.

"It's broken," Madyson said from the sofa, in the tone of someone delivering a verdict rather than bad news.

"It's out of tune and one key is stuck. Those are different problems." He had learned the distinction from Ms. Morningstar, who had a habit of announcing, mid-scale, "That is not a wrong note, that is a wrong finger," as though the difference were obvious and slightly moral. He had started lessons in September because Giuliana said piano was the one instrument you couldn't look cool failing at, and he had taken this as a dare, and now, eight months later, he owned the fact that a standard piano has 88 keys and could play the first four bars of something Ms. Morningstar called a bagatelle, which he'd had to look up and which he suspected she'd chosen because the word was funny.

He pressed the dead key again. Nothing. He pressed the walnut one. Crack. He tried them together, which produced half a walnut.

"So what's the plan?" Madyson came over and stood beside him with her hands in her pockets, which was her posture for pontificating. "Because I've heard Uncle Rick on this subject. He'll say leave it, he'll say the movers cost more than the piano, he'll say Dot would want us to be practical, and then he'll eat a sandwich about it."

"The plan is I want to hear it work. Once. Before Saturday." He said it before he'd decided it was true, which was how most of his wants arrived. "There's a guy at school, the one who fixes the auditorium piano. Giuliana knows him."

"Giuliana knows everyone. Giuliana's whole personality is knowing a guy."

The guy's name was irrelevant; everyone called him the Tuner, including teachers, which Ryan found ominous and Madyson found hilarious. He came Thursday after school with a canvas bag and an expression suggesting he'd been promised a piano and found a morass. He lifted the lid, played a glissando that made both of them wince, then pried the D loose from whatever had fused it, blew something out of the works, and began twisting pins with a tool like a small lever, ear tilted, listening to beats that Ryan could not hear and did not pretend to.

"That's not actually destitute," the Tuner said, working. "People say these old uprights are worthless. This one's just neglected. Different problems." He glanced at Ryan. "You play?"

"He counts," Madyson said.

"He plays four bars of a bagatelle," Ryan said, and when the Tuner finished and closed the lid, Ryan sat down and played those four bars, then the four after them, which he'd only practiced in his head on the bus, and they came out wrong but not broken, which was the distinction he trusted most now.

His mother came Saturday with the movers and stood in the doorway with her keys in her hand. Madyson was at the sofa. Ryan was still on the bench.

"Rick found a church that'll take it," she said. "It's not far."

He played the walnut key, which was now only slightly a walnut. "Can I come when they deliver it?"

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, using England and Portugal trading cloth and wine.
story:
Tristan had claimed the corner table in the library annex before first bell, three days running, because the economics exam on Thursday covered trade theory and he still could not hold the original example in his head. He knew it mattered. He knew there had been a book, and a year, and two countries, and two goods, and every time he reached for the details they slid apart like wet cards.

At lunch he found Drew in the cafeteria line, tray wobbling under a pile of fries that had no right to be that tall. "Quiz me," Tristan said. "Econ. Please. I'll owe you."

"You'll owe me," Drew repeated, but he put down his tray at the corner table anyway and pulled Tristan's notebook across without asking, which was how they had always worked. Tristan watched him read, watched his eyebrows climb. "You wrote England and Spain."

"I wrote England and somebody."

"Okay, so walk me through it. Who wrote the thing?"

"Ricardo." That much had stuck. "David Ricardo. He set out comparative advantage in a book, and the book used two countries trading cloth and wine. England and Portugal. The thing I keep losing is the year and the title."

Boston slid into the third chair uninvited, the way she did when a conversation looked like it might get obstreperous and she wanted a seat for it. "The year is 1817," she said. "And the title is enormous. On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. Mr. Ahmed made us write it out twice because he said the full title would show up on the exam and half of us would butcher it."

"You're sure," Tristan said.

"I copied it off the board and I still have the page."

She turned her binder around and there it was in her square handwriting, the year, the title, the names, cloth and wine, England and Portugal, arranged as if they had never once come apart in her head. Tristan copied it slowly, saying each piece under his breath, and when he got to the end he said it again from the top without looking. It held, this time, the way a knot holds once you've actually tied it rather than stared at the rope.

He thought of his grandfather, of a summer two years ago, a greenhouse behind the old house where the old man grew tomatoes he did not especially like and gave most of them away. Tristan had asked him once why he bothered, and his grandfather had said the woman next door kept bees, and the bees did their part, and the tomatoes did theirs, and neither of them had signed a contract. Tristan, fifteen and sure of himself, had called that symbiosis with the smugness of a boy who had just learned the word in biology, and his grandfather had laughed and said that was exactly what he'd meant, except that nobody had to explain it to the bees. He thought of that now, the two of them trading across a fence, each keeping what it was better at, and he thought of Portugal with its wine and England with its cloth, and the two ideas folded together in his mind like the halves of a book closing.

"After school," he said, "I want to try explaining it out loud. To you two. If I can explain it, I actually have it."

So at three-thirty they took the annex table by the window, and Tristan laid it out: Ricardo, 1817, the book with its long title, England and Portugal, cloth and wine, and how the strange part was that both countries gained even if one of them was better at making both things, which was the point his own notes kept smudging. Boston stopped him once to say he was rushing, and he slowed down and did that part again. Drew asked what happened if a country decided it wanted to make everything itself anyway, and Tristan said he didn't fully know, that the book must have an answer but he hadn't found it yet, and he would rather say that than make something up. Drew nodded like that was the right kind of answer, and Tristan noticed him write something in the margin of his own notebook, though he couldn't see what.

On Thursday the exam came back to front of the room in Mr. Ahmed's hands, and the short-answer section, question four, asked for the original example, and Tristan filled it in cleanly and felt the knot hold all the way to the end of the pen stroke.

Friday, the marks posted by the door. Tristan scanned the column for his name and found his mark, good, solid, what he'd earned. Then he looked for Drew's, out of curiosity, and found it four points higher. He turned around. "How? You asked me what the title was on Wednesday."

Drew held up his notebook, open to the margin where he had written, in small careful letters, the whole thing: 1817, the full title, cloth and wine, England and Portugal. "You said it out loud twice," he said. "I just wrote down what I heard."

Boston looked from one of them to the other and back. "So the country that was better at making both things," she said slowly, "still ended up trading."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
The bus dropped them at the quarry gate with instructions to stay inside the orange cones, which Christophe interpreted as a suggestion. Mr. Walker carried a tube of rolled paper under one arm the way other men carried newspapers, and Cameron trailed behind him trying to remember the exact words he had gotten wrong the day before. He needed this. The failed quiz sat in his folder like a stone, and the makeup explanation was due Monday, out loud, in front of everyone, on a graph he still could not read.

"Notice the benches," Mr. Walker said, meaning the flat steps cut into the rock wall, each one a year of digging, each one lower than the last. He unrolled the paper on a folding table near the water's edge and weighted the corners with stones. It was the Mauna Loa graph, carbon dioxide across decades, the line climbing and climbing, and stitched through the climbing, sawtooth wiggles, up and down, up and down, hundreds of them.

Cameron leaned over it and felt his stomach drop the way it had in class. The upward trend he could explain; molecules absorb heat and radiate it back, and more molecules mean more heat retained, like a blanket thickening. He had said that part fine. But the wiggles had undone him. He had told Mr. Walker they were probably errors in the instruments, noise in the data, and Mr. Walker had looked at him for a long second and written something in his book.

"What's wrong with it?" Janna came up beside him with her sandwich half-eaten in one hand. She was the kind of person who could look at a graph the way she looked at a cashier, with frank impatience.

"Nothing's wrong with it," Cameron said. "That's the problem. It's real and I can't explain it."

Christophe, who had wandered past the cones to stand on the lowest bench, cupped his hands around his mouth. "Come look at this wall, it goes down forever." His voice came back off the far side of the quarry, doubled. Mr. Walker said his name once, not loudly, and Christophe came back the way he had gone, hopping between stones, and if the teacher's even tone was meant to assuage anyone it did not work, because Janna had gone still watching the water.

They spread their lunches on the far end of the table so the graph would stay clean. Cameron ate without tasting. The wiggles ran up and down like teeth and he kept counting them, one per year, or maybe two, hard to tell at this scale, and every explanation he tried sounded like the last one, the wrong one. Error. Noise. Instrument drift. Each word felt like guessing at the shape of something in dark water.

Janna reached over and tapped the sawtooth with a ketchup-stained finger. "So it goes down a little every year and then back up. And down. If it's not the machine, something out there is breathing." She said it as a joke, and Cameron started to say that the atmosphere doesn't breathe, and then stopped with his mouth open, because down the slope behind the quarry fence the trees stood in their June thickness, whole hillsides of them, leaves out, everything green, and he remembered October, the same hillsides going bare, and November, the leaves blackening and flattening under rain.

"It's the plants," he said. "The Northern Hemisphere ones. When they grow, spring and summer, all those leaves take the carbon dioxide in, and that's when the line dips. Then autumn and winter, the leaves die and decay, and it all goes back out." He put his finger on one downward tooth. "Down here, that's summer. Everywhere, all at once, the whole top half of the planet." He followed the zigzag up. "And up here, winter. It breathes once a year and it never gets all the way back down, because underneath it, the whole curve is still climbing." Nobody said anything. Janna looked at the trees and then at the paper and then back at the trees, and Mr. Walker, who had been listening from the table's end while pretending to read his own copy, turned a page he had already read.

"It's not an error," Cameron said, mostly to himself, and then, because he wanted it on record before anyone could take it from him, "I said it was an error. I want to say that I was wrong about that." He was already working out how he would stand up Monday and trace one year of it with his finger, summer dip, winter rise, and then the next year, and the next, each breath a little higher than the last, the way the benches of the quarry stepped down and down toward water nobody had measured the depth of. Christophe had drifted back toward the cones. "This time it's fine," he called back over his shoulder, one foot already past the orange. "I just want to see the edge."

Mr. Walker rose from the table without hurry, and Cameron, still holding the corner of the graph down with a flat stone, watched the two of them, teacher and boy, stand together at the lip of the lowest bench, looking down.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
The restaurant was called Verano, and Loic told himself he had walked into harder rooms than this. He had not, exactly, but the telling was almost the same as the walking, and by the time the hostess led him past the kitchen doors he had nearly convinced himself that his hands were steady.

Mr. Shapiro met him at the back booth with a folder and a pen. He was the owner, small and quick, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair. "You're the one who emailed three times," he said. "I like persistence. Sit."

The interview went the way Loic had rehearsed it in the bathroom mirror, which is to say it went smoothly because most of it was not true. He said he had helped at his uncle's catering business, that he was comfortable under pressure, that cash handling was familiar to him. Mr. Shapiro nodded along, contextualizing each claim against some private ledger of what a busboy actually needed to know, and apparently the ledger came out favorable, because he slid the folder across the table and said, "You're hired. Weekends to start. Fill these out and you can begin Saturday."

The folder held a stack of forms, and the stack held, near its middle, a page that stopped Loic cold. Form W-4, the header said. Employee's Withholding Certificate. He read the first line twice and understood none of it better the second time. There were steps, allowances, a worksheet. The restaurant noise, which had seemed pleasantly cosmopolitan a minute ago, silverware and three languages at the bar, now felt like static.

He excused himself to the vestibule and texted Emeric, who was theoretically in the same economics class. Do you know what a W-4 is. Emeric replied with a shrugging emoji and then, usefully: kirans dad does payroll. Loic texted Kiran, and Kiran called him back in under a minute, whispering, because he was supposed to be in study hall.

"It's the withholding form," Kiran said. "When you start a job in the US, you fill out a Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to take out of each paycheck. That's the whole thing. Your mom or dad signs off if you're under eighteen, I think, but you're eighteen, right?"

"I'm eighteen," Loic said. "So I just, what, put one for the allowances?"

"I don't know the allowances. My dad does them. Ask your mom."

Here was the problem, the one Loic had been carrying since the booth. His mother worked nights at the hospital and slept through the afternoon, and more to the point, he did not want to tell her he had a job at all, because telling her meant telling her he needed money, and telling her he needed money meant explaining what the money was for, and he was not ready to explain the money. He had told himself the two things were separate, the job and the reason for the job, but standing in the vestibule he could feel the causality linking them anyway, a thin wire he had been pretending wasn't there.

He went back to the booth. Mr. Shapiro had moved on to folding napkins, a small mountain of them. Loic sat and looked at the form. Step one, name and address. Step two was the one that scared him, the part he couldn't bluff. He thought of the uncle's catering business, which existed, which had never employed him, and he understood suddenly that he was about to do the same arithmetic on the form that he had done in the interview, and that the form was different, because the form went to the government.

"Question," he said. "The part about the allowances. I've never done this. My uncle paid me cash, so this is, this is actually my first real job." Saying it out loud was easier than he had expected, like setting down something heavy on purpose rather than dropping it.

Mr. Shapiro took off his glasses. "First job," he said. "The interview said catering experience."

"Helping out. Once. Mostly I carried chairs." Loic looked at the napkins, the table, anywhere. "I can carry chairs here too. And trays. I learn fast, you already know that part's true, you saw me carry three plates through the kitchen without dropping anything on the tour."

Mr. Shapiro folded one more napkin, creased it flat with the edge of his hand, and set it on the mountain. "You'll fill out the W-4 with your mother or father tonight, before Saturday, or no Saturday. That part's not optional. And the lying, we'll discuss after you've worked a month, if you last a month." He tapped the form. "Read the steps in order. It's easier than it looks."

Loic nodded. Outside, in the parking lot, he pulled out his phone and scrolled to his mother's name, thumb hovering, the restaurant's warm light on the glass behind him. He pressed call.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking or cycling on most days, lowers blood pressure in many people, including those who already have hypertension.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around her grandfather's arm until he winced, then the machine beeped out its numbers with the enthusiasm of a slot machine paying badly. Isabella copied them onto the back of a grocery receipt: 158 over 96. She was starting a nursing program in the fall, and her mother had suggested, in the tone of someone assigning homework over summer break, that she might as well learn the machine at Grandpa's house since he refused to learn it himself.

"It says thank you for your patience," she said.

"It can wait longer than I can," her grandfather said.

She knew the numbers mattered but not how to read them, so she texted Dominik, who had spent the whole senior year working at the pharmacy on Miller Street and acted like it. He sent back a photo of a laminated card. Top number, the pressure when the heart beats. Bottom number, between beats. Then ranges, color coded like a weather map. She held the receipt up beside the phone screen. 158 over 96 sat squarely in the red zone, the one labeled hypertension. The word looked official and slightly accusatory, like a parking ticket.

"You're in the red," she told her grandfather.

"I'm in my kitchen," he said. "The red is the kettle."

She called the pharmacy anyway, because a card could not argue back and her grandfather could, extensively. Dominik answered on the second ring and put her on speaker while he counted pill bottles, which she could hear clicking like a slow clock. She read him the numbers. He said that was high, that one reading wasn't a diagnosis, and that her grandfather should actually see a doctor rather than be diagnosed by a girl holding a grocery receipt. She said she understood that. Then, quieter, she asked what actually helped.

"Regular aerobic exercise," Dominik said. "Brisk walking, cycling, most days. It lowers blood pressure in a lot of people, and that includes people who already have hypertension." He said he'd read it in the patient handouts enough times to have it tattooed. She wrote it on the receipt under the numbers, then crossed out nothing, because it was all she had.

The problem she could not amortize over the summer was this: her grandfather had not deliberately walked anywhere since 1994, and he treated the stationary bike in the basement, a wedding gift from her late grandmother, as furniture. It held a stack of National Geographics arranged in strict chronology, oldest at the bottom, which was the only exercise it got. When Isabella proposed evening walks, he delivered a parsimonious reply: "No." She let it sit. Then she asked whether he would walk with her, not for his arteries but because the route past the reservoir had a heron he'd mentioned once in March and never again, and she wanted to see if it was still there.

He looked at the receipt, which she had left on the table like evidence. He looked at the machine, which was still plugged in and humming faintly, waiting for a wrist. "If the heron's gone," he said, "we walk home without discussion."

They walked that evening, briskly by his standard, which was strolling by anyone else's. He carried nothing; she carried his jacket in case he got cold, which he said he would not, and then put on at the halfway point without comment. The heron was there, standing in the shallows with the patience of something that had also refused all advice. Her grandfather watched it for a while and asked her what the top number was called again. Systolic, she said. And the bottom. Diastolic. He repeated each word once, under his breath, the way he memorized the names of birds.

They agreed on a schedule on the walk home: most days, after dinner, before the news, rain permitting, and rain not always permitting. At the door he let her take his blood pressure again, out of what he called fairness to the machine. The numbers came back lower, though she knew from Dominik's card that one evening meant almost nothing yet, and she said so. "Then we'll give it more than one evening," her grandfather said, and rolled his sleeve back down. "The heron wasn't built in a day either."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
The robotics room smelled like solder and cold pizza, and the regional qualifier was eleven days away. Ryder stood at the parts cabinet counting motor mounts for the third time because Gianluca had not delivered the revised arm code he had promised, and without it the mounts were just metal waiting for instructions that would never come. In the practice log, next to Tuesday's date, was a blank line where the third revision should have been recorded. Ryder had already drafted a message in his head, something about how some people clearly did not care whether the team went to regionals at all, and it felt good and terrible at the same time, like a fist already clenched.

"You're doing the face," Fatima said from the far table, where she was splicing the sensor harness. "The one where you're rehearsing a fight."

"I'm rehearsing honesty," Ryder said.

"Those aren't the same thing." She set down the strippers and pulled a folded handout from her binder, the one Ms. Takahashi had left on the resource shelf after the leadership workshop nobody had attended. "I read this last night because I have to review your chassis notes and I didn't want to murder you either. Look." She smoothed the page on the table so he could see the diagram, three boxes connected by arrows, labeled situation, behavior, impact. "It's from the Center for Creative Leadership," she said. "It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model."

Ryder read the handout twice while Fatima went back to the harness. The model, as far as he could tell, wanted you to name when the thing happened, what the person actually did, and what effect it had. It sounded almost too simple, the kind of thing that would dissolve the second you were actually angry at somebody. He tried it out on paper, privately, in the margin of the practice log. "You're lazy" became, under the model's pressure, something with dates in it: on Tuesday, at the build session, the revision he had promised did not arrive, and the arm team spent two hours blocked. He noticed that writing it down forced him to check whether it was even true, and he found that it was, mostly, though he also found, less comfortably, that he had never actually asked Gianluca what was going on at home. That part the model said nothing about. He turned the margin fact over for a while without deciding what to do with it.

Gianluca came in at four with his backpack slung wrong and his hoodie damp from the rain, and he went straight for the laptop as if nothing were missing. Ryder stood up before his rehearsed vitriolic version could regroup. His stomach did something he would need a few hours to metabolize, but his mouth started anyway.

"Tuesday, at the build session," he said, and his voice came out steadier than he expected. "The arm revision you said would be ready wasn't there, and the arm team spent two hours blocked waiting on it. That put us a full day behind for the qualifier." He stopped. That was the whole model, situation, behavior, impact, and it felt strangely small now that it was out loud, small and clean.

Gianluca's hands paused over the keyboard. "My mom's in the hospital," he said, not looking up. "Since Monday. I was going to tell you and then I kept not telling you." The room hummed with the printer and the rain against the high windows. Ryder sat down on the stool beside him, and after a while he said the revision could wait until Thursday if that was what Gianluca needed, and that he should have asked sooner instead of filling the silence with his own story about laziness. Fatima brought over two of the spare harness clips and said nothing, which was its own kind of kindness. What Ryder could not figure out, even later, was whether the model had made him honest or whether it had only given him a shape to be honest in, and whether the shape mattered if the words underneath were still partly guesswork. He watched Gianluca open the code editor and begin, slowly, to type.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population, pointing to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care.
story:
The rain had been falling since noon, and by evening it had inured them all to dampness in a way none of them had chosen. Landon sat with his back against a cedar stump, his phone balanced on his knee, its charge at eleven percent, and the assignment sheet folded into a soggy square in his jacket pocket. Mr. Gupta had been clear at the trailhead: the analysis was due when they reached the parking lot tomorrow at ten, submitted by phone before the bus left, and no exceptions for weather, mood, or dead batteries. The rest of the group had claimed the good tarp. Landon had claimed a rock.

"You're going to fail geography because of a tree stump," Elie said, crouching under the edge of the tarp with a bag of trail mix he was guarding like evidence.

"I'm going to fail geography because I don't understand the graphs." Landon held the phone out into the gray light. On the screen was the population pyramid of Japan, printed on the sheet, bars fanning out from a center line, ages running up the side, millions running across the bottom. His task was to look at the shape and say what the country would need in twenty years, more schools or more nursing homes, and to defend the answer. He had a guess. He hated that it was only a guess.

Klara crossed the wet gravel and sat down beside him, pulling her own sheet from a plastic sleeve, which Landon noticed and did not comment on. She had drawn arrows on hers. He had drawn nothing. "Okay," she said, "look at the actual shape. Look at the base."

He looked. The lowest bars, the youngest ages, were short. The bars above them, the middle of the pyramid, were wide, much wider, so the whole figure bulged in its middle like a barrel and pinched at the bottom. That was not what a pyramid was supposed to do. A pyramid was supposed to be wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, like the ones in the antiquated textbook in the school library that nobody had replaced since the printing, but the shape on his page had stopped cooperating with its own name.

"So the bottom is narrower than the middle," he said slowly. "Fewer kids than people of, what, working age. That keeps going, the young part keeps shrinking."

"Which means what later?"

He followed the shape upward with one finger, the middle bars thick, the top bars thin, the whole wide middle drifting toward the top of the chart like something rising in water. Fewer children being born, a large population growing older. He thought of his grandfather, who lived in a care home with a courtyard the staff called the garden, and who once asked him, on a bad afternoon, who would be around to help when Landon himself was old. Landon had not had an answer. He had been seventeen and had changed the subject.

"If the base is narrower than the middle," he said, "birth rates are falling, the population's aging. In twenty years that country doesn't need more schools. It needs nursing homes. Elder care. That's the whole answer, isn't it?"

"For that country," Klara said. "Now look at yours."

He unfolded his second sheet, the pyramid for his own country, and held the two pages side by side in the failing light. His own was still a pyramid, wide at the base, but the bottom bars were thinner than the ones just above them, thinner than they would have been a generation ago. The shape was beginning to do what the Japanese shape had already done. He felt something shift in his thinking, two pictures sliding together: the barrel-shaped chart and the courtyard with its benches, the abstract bars and the concrete question his grandfather had actually asked him. The substrate beneath the assignment, he realized, was not paper. It was people, arranged into decades.

"Elie," Landon called. "Come here. Tell me if this is right."

Elie came, chewing. Landon laid the pages flat on the stump and explained it once, cleanly, the narrow base, the falling birth rates, the aging population, the nursing homes rising in demand while the schools emptied. Elie looked at the pages, then at him, and said, "That sounds right, but you're the one who has to write it, and your phone's at eight percent."

"Then I write it now." He typed with cold thumbs, and the harder problem surfaced as he typed: what to say about his own country, whose pyramid was only beginning to narrow. He could state the trend, but not when it would matter, or how bad it would get, or who would staff the care homes if the working middle kept shrinking. The shape told him the direction. It did not tell him the schedule. He wrote a paragraph saying exactly that, that the answer was confident for Japan and honest but uncertain for home, and let it stand.

Rain tapped the tarp all night. At 9:40 in the morning, boots muddy, Mr. Gupta walking the line of students checking phones, Landon pressed submit at 9:52 with two percent battery remaining. The screen went white, then confirmed, then went dark for good. Elie clapped him on the shoulder, and Klara said, "Read mine at the bus window and tell me if I got the aging part wrong." Landon slid the dead phone into his pocket and followed her toward the parking lot.
